Article Title: In 1816, Kentucky Shakers built a dwelling where newcomers learned about the community; the last surviving North Lot building is now getting a $1.5M restoration to reopen by 2029
Article Text:
An 1816 dwelling gets a second life

What the North Lot once represented

Shaker believers in Mercer County began dismantling a frame house on December 16, 1816, to build a new dwelling about a mile northeast of their village centre. The move was deliberate. The Shaker community was growing, and they needed a proper place for new converts to live and learn about Shaker life. The new building welcomed seekers, those who were curious about the doctrines of Mother Ann Lee, the founder of the community. For over a century, the North Lot Family Dwelling served as a place where people decided whether to join the community.Two centuries later, that building stands nearly empty, its structural integrity compromised by decades of neglect. However, Kentucky's preservation community has decided that it deserves a resurrection. A $1.5 million restoration has begun, and by 2029, the North Lot Family Dwelling will reopen, this time as a gathering space for different reasons, of course.The 210-year-old Shaker building that once served as a home for newcomers is being restored in a $1.5 million project, with plans to welcome visitors again by 2029. Shaker Village has received a $750,000 federal grant through the Save America's Treasures programme from the Historic Preservation Fund, administered by the National Park Service and the Department of the Interior, to support the restoration of the historic North Lot Family Dwelling, one of the most significant structures within the Village's 3,000-acre National Historic Landmark.“This is a transformative moment for Shaker Village,” Billy Rankin, Shaker Village President & CEO, said in a press release. “The North Lot Family Dwelling tells a powerful story about how the Shakers formed their community and connected with their fellow Kentuckians throughout the 19th century. Restoring this building allows that story to be shared in a way that has never been possible before. Plus, it will act as the ‘front porch’ of the Village since its placement along historic Highway 68 is the first Shaker structure many see when approaching the Village. ”The building is currently at risk due to structural and water damage. The restoration will be done via a three-phase approach, which includes structural repairs, masonry and exterior restoration, and full upgrades to mechanical systems.The total restoration will cost an estimated $1.5 million. The federal grant has been matched by funding from the Team Kentucky GRANT Program, private donor contributions, and in-kind support from Shaker Village's preservation team. The restoration will be complete within three years, with plans to reopen the North Lot Family Dwelling in 2029.The Shaker settlement at Pleasant Hill grew rapidly in the early 1800s. New converts arrived in waves, drawn by reports of successful communal farming, orderly worship, and a faith that promised salvation through confession and celibacy. The community needed intake stations. Housing was scarce, but inviting newcomers into established family units was not an option. So they built several dwellings, and the North Lot became one of two gathering orders at Pleasant Hill, a place where visitors could apprentice in communal life before choosing permanent membership. People who chose to commit were moved to the village, into one of the larger family dwellings that still dot the 3,000-acre landscape today.The North Lot once had about a dozen buildings. Many lived, worked, and followed their spiritual paths there. While some converted, others left. This North Lot building, now awaiting a second life, is the only one standing. It is a three-storey timber-frame building that had five bedrooms, a full kitchen, and a large sitting area that doubled as meeting space.Families lived, worked, and assessed their spiritual readiness there. Some converted. Many left. The building that survives was three storeys, with sturdy timber-frame construction, designed to accommodate a rotating population of uncertain believers. This is where the newcomers experienced Shaker routines like communal meals, work assignments, and worship practices. The building functioned as both residence and classroom.By the time Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill acquired the North Lot property in 1966, the Shaker community at Pleasant Hill had long since ceased to operate as a religious community. In the late 1970s, restoration began and was completed in 1981. From the following year, the building hosted retreats, guests, and small groups in a quiet setting. This arrangement lasted until 2008. That's when U.S. Highway 68 effectively erased the North Lot from the visitor experience. The building was later closed, and maintenance was neglected. By 2016, the building was in serious disrepair and at risk of further deterioration.
Article Summary: The North Lot Family Dwelling was built on December 16, 1816, by Shaker believers in Mercer County, Kentucky. It was a three-storey timber-frame building that had five bedrooms, a full kitchen, and a large sitting area that doubled as meeting space. For over a century, the North Lot served as a place where people decided whether to join the community.

Article Title: Volunteers spent 16 years restoring a damaged Arizona desert; 133 native plant species now thrive where invasive grass once ruled
Article Text:
16 years of restoring an 18-acre Arizona desert

Native trees helped rebuild the damaged desert

Water harvesting helped the desert hold on to rain

Discarded Christmas trees became an erosion-control tool

Buffelgrass declined as native habitat returned

An 18-acre stretch of Arizona desert that was once heavily disturbed and overrun by invasive buffelgrass has been transformed through 16 years of sustained restoration work by volunteers and conservation partners. The Waterman Restoration Project, located on Bureau of Land Management land within Ironwood Forest National Monument near Marana, began in 2010 after earlier attempts to control the invasive grass failed to produce lasting results. Volunteers helped reintroduce native trees, slow erosion, capture rainwater and suppress buffelgrass across the damaged site. The results have become increasingly visible over the years. The Arizona Native Plant Society now records 133 native plant species at the site, alongside more than 2,000 established native trees. Restoration continues, with volunteers still working to improve the desert habitat.The Waterman Restoration Project occupies an 18-acre desert bajada in southern Arizona, an area historically characterised by native Sonoran Desert vegetation. The site suffered major disturbance in 1981 when mining entrepreneur Harlow Jones bulldozed the land, including an approximately one-kilometre airstrip, according to an Arizona Native Plant Society technical paper.Jones later planted buffelgrass on the property, and by the early 2000s the disturbed area had become heavily dominated by the invasive grass. The Bureau of Land Management subsequently removed the unauthorised occupant and began efforts to address the degraded landscape. Sierra Club volunteers manually removed buffelgrass between 2005 and 2009, while BLM contractors also used herbicide. These measures reduced the grass temporarily but did not stop its return. The Arizona Native Plant Society began sustained restoration at the site in 2010.A major part of the restoration involved bringing back native vegetation without creating a conventional irrigated planting scheme. In 2010, BLM heavy equipment was used to reshape parts of the 18-acre site, fill erosion channels and create terraces that could slow and spread stormwater. Volunteers collected seeds from nearby native plants, including whitethorn acacia, foothill palo verde and ironwood, before planting them across the site. More than 2,000 tree seedlings emerged by September that year, and more than 2,000 native desert trees had become established by 2016. The trees were grown from locally collected seed and were not irrigated. Volunteers also spread more than 300 truckloads of tree branches over bare ground. The woody material helped shade the soil, retain residual moisture and create conditions in which native plants could establish. The restoration has since expanded beyond the original tree planting effort, with the Arizona Native Plant Society recording 133 native plant species at the site.Rainfall is highly variable in the Sonoran Desert, making the ability to slow and retain stormwater particularly important for restoration. Volunteers have constructed more than 150 simple water-harvesting structures at Waterman, including one-rock dams and rocked waterways designed to reduce the speed of runoff and spread water across the landscape. The project also used a backhoe to create water-retention dimples across about two acres of compacted gravel, giving rainfall more opportunity to soak into the ground rather than rapidly flowing away. Native plants and seeds began emerging from these areas within a year. The approach is based largely on passive water harvesting rather than regular irrigation. By modifying how water moves across the damaged landscape, the project has created better conditions for native vegetation to survive and spread. Volunteers continue to repair and add water-harvesting features as part of the long-term restoration work.One of the project's more unusual interventions came after a major storm in September 2022. About 3.5 inches of rain fell in roughly three hours, carving a channel approximately 500 feet long, three feet wide and three feet deep through the upper part of the restoration area. Rather than relying solely on conventional infrastructure, volunteers began packing discarded Christmas trees into the channel in early 2023. The trees were placed end-to-end and packed into the trench after their above-ground dried growth was removed. Arizona Native Plant Society monitoring found no runoff in the channel during rainfall events exceeding 0.25 inches during 2023. Another 50 Christmas trees were added during the winter of 2024, with further additions reported in 2025 and 2026. The channel has gradually begun filling in and developing a more meandering form. The technique is a site-specific restoration measure intended to slow water and trap sediment, rather than evidence that discarded Christmas trees are universally suitable for erosion control.Controlling buffelgrass has remained an essential part of the project because the invasive grass can outcompete native desert vegetation and increase wildfire risk in Sonoran Desert ecosystems. During the first year of sustained restoration, three to five volunteers carried out spot spraying several times a week between August and October. The amount of herbicide used fell sharply as the infestation declined, from about 234 gallons in 2010 to 74 gallons in 2011, 45 gallons in 2012 and 10 gallons in 2013. Since 2015, annual use has generally been only about three to five gallons. The Arizona Native Plant Society and BLM report that fewer than 150 buffelgrass plants have emerged at the site in a season since 2022. Meanwhile, the restored landscape now supports 133 recorded native plant species and more than 2,000 established native trees. More than 75 salvaged saguaros have also been transplanted onto the site since 2021. More than 7,000 volunteer hours have contributed to the project, and restoration remains ongoing rather than being considered finished.
Article Summary: The Waterman Restoration Project began in 2010 after earlier attempts to control the invasive grass failed to produce lasting results. Volunteers helped reintroduce native trees, slow erosion, capture rainwater and suppress buffelgrass across the damaged site. The Arizona Native Plant Society records 133 native plant species at the site, alongside more than 2,000 established native trees.

Article Title: In 2017, USGS released 72.57 kg of red dye into Idaho’s Kootenai River in 90 seconds; aircraft 1,000 metres above mapped the plume in 0.5-metre pixels to study river dispersion
Article Text:
An aircraft followed the plume from above (Representational AI image)

Following the dye through the water

An aircraft followed the plume from above

What the experiment was trying to show

In September 2017, the US Geological Survey (USGS) carried out an unusual experiment on Idaho’s Kootenai River. Researchers released 72.57 kg (160 pounds) of Rhodamine WT dye into the river and then followed its movement through the water. The aim was to understand how a substance spreads as it travels through a flowing river.According to USGS, the dye was released from a single point at the Kootenai Tribal Fish Hatchery on September 26, 2017. The entire release took just 90 seconds. Researchers then had to track what happened to the dye as it moved downstream and spread across the river.They used two methods to follow the plume. Instruments placed in the river measured the dye directly, while an aircraft flew over the Kootenai River the following day, capturing images of the plume from above. Together, the two sets of observations helped researchers study how the dye changed as it moved through the river.The aircraft carried a hyperspectral imaging system, which can record information from different parts of the electromagnetic spectrum rather than taking an ordinary photograph. It flew about 1,000 metres above the ground while making several passes along the river. The images showed the changing plume across the river channel.The aerial observations were backed by measurements taken directly from the river. Researchers used five water quality sondes to track the Rhodamine WT dye.Four of the instruments were placed at fixed locations in the river. They recorded how the dye concentration changed over time as the plume passed those points. The fifth instrument was placed on a jet boat, allowing researchers to move through the river and measure the dye at different locations.The jet boat measurements were particularly useful because the dye did not simply move in one straight line downstream. Researchers recorded its concentration along the river and across different sections of the channel. This helped them see how the plume changed as it spread through the water.The field measurements continued for nearly 40 hours after the dye was released. During that period, the river flow remained relatively steady. The USGS measured an average discharge of 198.4 cubic metres per second at the gaging station near the Tribal Hatchery. The researchers also recorded the location and time of each measurement.On September 27, Quantum Spatial Inc. collected hyperspectral images of the Kootenai River using an ITRES CASI 1500H system mounted on a manned Cessna Caravan aircraft.The aircraft followed shorter flight lines along the river during multiple passes. This allowed researchers to capture the dye plume at different stages of its movement rather than relying on a single image.The system recorded 48 spectral bands between 380 and 1,050 nanometres. The images had pixels measuring 0.5 metres, giving researchers a detailed view of the river surface and the changing plume.The images were then processed so they could be compared with the measurements collected in the river. The data were corrected for atmospheric effects and converted into a form that could be analysed alongside the field observations.This comparison was an important part of the experiment. Researchers wanted to know whether an aircraft could provide useful information about dye concentrations in the river, instead of relying only on instruments placed in the water.The experiment was not simply about photographing a coloured patch moving through the Kootenai River. The researchers were testing whether remote sensing could help measure the concentration of a tracer dye as it spread.The timing of the aircraft flights was recorded so the images could be matched with Rhodamine WT measurements taken from the river at corresponding times. This gave researchers a way to compare what the aircraft saw from above with what instruments measured in the water.The field measurements also had another role. They could be used to support and validate hydrodynamic numerical models that simulate river flow and the movement and dispersion of material through water. The data also supported Lagrangian particle tracking, a method used to study how particles move with flowing water.The USGS published the hyperspectral data from the experiment in 2018. Related research was later published in the Journal of Ecohydraulics in 2019 under the title “Remote sensing of tracer dye concentrations to support dispersion studies in river channels”.
Article Summary: Researchers released 72.57 kg of Rhodamine WT dye into the Kootenai River. They then followed its movement through the water. Instruments placed in the river measured the dye directly. An aircraft flew over the river the following day, capturing images of the plume from above.

Article Title: In 1992, a partnership began rebuilding Lake Havasu’s declining fish habitat; 90 acres of artificial habitat helped improve about 875 acres of coves, with habitat now created across 124 coves
Article Text:
During its first decade, the partnership installed approximately 90 acres of artificial habitat, improving about 875 acres of cove complexes.

A partnership built around conservation

Science behind the habitat

From local brush to underwater habitat

Volunteers make the difference

Lake Havasu is famous for striped bass, redear sunfish, world-class fishing tournaments and unforgettable days on the water. But beneath that success is a decades-long conservation effort that many visitors never see. For more than three decades, the Lake Havasu Fisheries Improvement Program has worked to strengthen aquatic habitat, improve recreational fishing and support the lake’s fishery and surrounding economy. The partnership formed in 1992 with a goal of enhancing the natural character of the reservoir while increasing fish species richness and strengthening predator-prey interactions to improve angling opportunities.Led by Bureau of Land Management Lake Havasu Field Office fisheries biologist Rachel Wirick, the program brings together federal, state and local organizations, along with dedicated volunteers. Partners include the Bureau of Land Management, Bureau of Reclamation, U.S. Geological Survey, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Arizona Game and Fish, Arizona State Parks and Trails, California Department of Fish and Wildlife, Anglers United, the Lake Havasu Divers Association and the Lake Havasu Marine Association.During its first decade, the partnership installed approximately 90 acres of artificial habitat, improving about 875 acres of cove complexes.“The BLM Colorado River District is overjoyed to have a fisheries biologist as knowledgeable and committed to the preservation and conservation of this very unique aquatic habitat as Rachel,” said Lake Havasu Field Office Manager Amanda Dodson. “She is a true example of the passion, dedication, and integrity required to develop and foster community level partnerships.”Lake Havasu is an artificial reservoir that lacks much of the natural woody structure fish depend on. The program addresses that challenge by creating habitat using PVC pipes, snow fencing and concrete reef balls across 124 coves managed by the BLM along the Arizona and California shorelines.The habitat serves several important ecological functions. Decomposing vegetation provides a surface for algae and zooplankton, helping support the lower levels of the food web and species such as shad and young fish. As vegetation breaks down, it leaves spaces where smaller fish can shelter from predators. Those concentrations of prey, in turn, attract sportfish such as bass and catfish, creating productive areas for anglers.Natural brush is an important part of the program, too. Donated palm fronds and tree branches from local landscapers are bundled with steel strapping at Partners Point. Sandbags are then attached so the bundles can be transported by boat and placed in 15 to 18 feet of water — deep enough to remain accessible to fish while staying out of the way of boat traffic.The program can install as many as 800 brush bundles annually. The effort not only creates habitat but also diverts landscaping material from local landfills.The program’s success depends heavily on its volunteer team, many of whom are retired anglers. They provide the hands-on labor needed to build bundles, load boats, install habitat and maintain existing structures.Since its management plan evolved in 2005, the partnership has expanded its focus to include monitoring, maintenance and long-term habitat productivity. Projects have included additional public fishing facilities, endangered fish monitoring and continued assessment of artificial reefs and supplemental brush.Images Courtesy: Bureau of Land Management and istock
Article Summary: The Lake Havasu Fisheries Improvement Program has worked to strengthen aquatic habitat, improve recreational fishing and support the lake’s fishery and surrounding economy. The partnership formed in 1992 with a goal of enhancing the natural character of the reservoir while increasing fish species richness and strengthening predator-prey interactions.

Article Title: In Gateshead, water trapped 150 metres below the city in abandoned coal mines now heats 350 homes and public buildings
Article Text:
Image AI generated

Mine water heat pump powers Gateshead buildings

Why does mine water get warmer with depth

Image AI generated

What is the Gateshead living laboratory studying

Water trapped deep beneath Gateshead is now helping heat hundreds of homes and public buildings, turning former coal mine workings into a source of heat for the city. The water lies around 150 metres below Gateshead town centre, where a 6-megawatt water-source heat pump extracts its heat and feeds it into an existing district heating network. According to the Mining Remediation Authority, the system went live on 29 March 2023 after about three years of work and is the largest mine water heat network in Great Britain. More than 5 kilometres of heat-network pipes carry the heat to buildings including Gateshead College, the Baltic Arts Centre, several offices and 350 council-owned homes. The network is also planned to reach another 270 privately owned homes, alongside a new conference centre and hotel development. The project is also being studied through the Gateshead Living Laboratory, where boreholes and monitoring equipment collect data on the mine water system.A 6 megawatt water-source heat pump recovers heat from the mine water and transfers it into the district heating network. The heated water is then distributed through more than 5 kilometres of heat-network pipes to connected buildings.The network currently supplies heat to several types of buildings across Gateshead.These include Gateshead College, the Baltic Arts Centre, several offices and 350 council-owned homes. The source states that the system is also planned to serve another 270 privately owned homes, as well as a new conference centre and a hotel development.Mine water becomes warmer with increasing depth because of what the Mining Remediation Authority describes as a ‘geothermal gradient’. Mine water temperatures generally range from 10°C to 20°C, although they can reach 40°C at depths of around 1 kilometre. Water can be brought to the surface through boreholes, shafts or adits, before heat exchangers and pumps recover its heat. The authority says mine water temperatures are not affected by seasonal variations. It describes mine water as a potential source of “renewable, secure, low carbon heating for buildings in coalfield areas”, with the right support and sustainable management.The Gateshead mine water heating network is part of a wider research project known as the Gateshead Living Laboratory. The initiative is designed to collect evidence that supports future licensing, management and wider use of mine water heat schemes. It is located near three mine water heat schemes in the North East of England.With support from Gateshead Council, researchers drilled four boreholes and installed monitoring equipment to gather data. The information is available as open-access data for researchers, regulators, stakeholders and academic institutions. The government says the work will help researchers study the thermal and hydrogeological interactions between multiple mine water heat schemes in the Walker mining block in Tyne and Wear.
Article Summary: A 6 megawatt water-source heat pump recovers heat from the mine water and transfers it into the district heating network. The heated water is then distributed through more than 5 kilometres of heat-network pipes to connected buildings. The network currently supplies heat to several types of buildings across Gateshead. These include Gateshead College, the Baltic Arts Centre, several offices and 350 council-owned homes.

Article Title: Before 9/11, families could walk passengers to airport gates; 25 years later a TSA pilot is bringing that back at 13 US airports for PreCheck members
Article Text:
For many travellers, the biggest benefit is spending more time with loved ones before or after a flight.

How the gate pass works

Security rules remain in place

Why travellers want the option

Before 9/11, families could walk passengers to airport gates; 25 years later a TSA pilot is bringing that back at 13 US airports for PreCheck membersPeople flying through Mesa Gateway Airport in Arizona can now have family members or friends meet them at the gate, even if those visitors are not travelling themselves. According to Fox 10, the airport is among 13 in the US taking part in a pilot programme that allows eligible people to pass through airport security without having a flight ticket.The programme, called Gateside by TSA PreCheck, brings back an experience many American travellers remember from before the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. At that time, people without tickets could travel through the airport and walk with passengers to the gate.That changed after 9/11, when airport security rules became much stricter. Access beyond security checkpoints was generally limited to people with a plane ticket. Now, the pilot programme is testing whether some non-ticketed visitors can once again enter the gate area under existing security rules.Mesa Gateway Airport has been part of the programme for about a week, according to Ryan Smith, the airport's director of communications. "We're only a week into the program," Smith said. "It's been a huge success." The programme gives approved visitors a single-day gate pass, but they must meet certain requirements before they can enter the secure area.The programme is available to people who have TSA PreCheck. Those who want to use it must inform the airport that they want a pass one to three days before the day of the flight.If the request is approved, the visitor receives the gate pass by email. They can then take the pass and their identification to the airport and go through the security checkpoint.People entering the gate area through the programme are subject to the same security restrictions as ticketed passengers.That security requirement has also been an important part of the discussion around the programme. While many travellers interviewed by FOX 10 said they would welcome the chance to enter the gate area without a ticket, some people said they were concerned about any change to airport security procedures.One traveller said they preferred stronger security measures, even if that meant spending more time going through TSA screening."Oh yeah," the traveller said. "I'm actually scared when they don't find something like hairspray or water in my bottle. I think the more security the better. I mean I don't care how long it takes me to get through TSA."For many passengers, the biggest benefit is being able to stay with relatives or friends for longer before a flight or meet them immediately after they arrive.People interviewed at Mesa Gateway Airport said the option could be especially useful for families and passengers who need help at the airport.One traveller said the return of gate access would be welcome. "I do miss that a lot," the person said. "That was definitely something to get off the airplane and see somebody right there. I kinda miss doing that."Another person pointed to the needs of older passengers, saying a family member could enter the secure area and help with bags or other needs.The programme could also help families in situations where a child is travelling between divorced parents. One traveller explained that allowing a parent to walk a child all the way to the gate could prevent the child from having to continue alone after passing through security.Another example involved a traveller with autism. "We had a traveler that has a son that's on the spectrum, and they just wanted to go through the process and kind of get used to going through the airport prior to having that ticket booked," the traveller said.
Article Summary: TSA pilot programme allows non-ticketed visitors to enter gate area without tickets. Mesa Gateway Airport in Arizona is one of 13 US airports taking part in the programme. The programme is available to people who have TSA PreCheck. Travellers say they would welcome the chance to enter the gate area.

Article Title: 30 Kansas inmates donate $4,267 from their own funds to pay down local children's lunch debt
Article Text:
Kansas inmates raise $4,267 from their own funds

Donation was presented to school superintendent

Reaching Out From Within focuses on rehabilitation

Many participants understood the struggle with hunger

Donation highlights both kindness and a wider problem

Nearly 30 incarcerated men in northwest Kansas have donated $4,267 to help pay down unpaid school meal debt at Norton Community Schools, turning money raised inside a correctional facility into support for children in their local community. Members of Reaching Out From Within, a rehabilitation programme at Norton Correctional Facility, raised $3,810 from their personal funds during a spring and summer fundraiser. Kansas Department of Corrections staff added another $457, bringing the total to $4,267. The donation was presented to Norton Community Schools Superintendent Corey Roy on August 3 and will help provide meals for children whose families have struggled to pay their school accounts.The fundraiser began after members of Reaching Out From Within learned that Norton Community Schools, USD 211, had accumulated about $6,000 in unsettled meal debt by the end of the 2025-26 school year. The debt had built up from breakfast and lunch served to students whose families were facing food insecurity and could not pay their children's accounts. Rather than simply discussing the problem, members of the prison-based programme decided to organise a fundraiser.They eventually collected $3,810 from their own personal funds, while Kansas Department of Corrections staff contributed another $457. The resulting $4,267 donation covered roughly 71% of the reported $6,000 debt.The money was formally presented during a ceremony at Norton Correctional Facility on August 3, when nearly 30 incarcerated men gathered to hand the donation to Norton Community Schools Superintendent Corey Roy. The facility said the money was intended to be "paid forward" and used to help local children fuel their day and remain focused and energised during the school year. Roy said he was moved by the men's desire to make a positive impact on other people in their community. He also spoke with participants individually and as a group, telling them that their actions had made a positive difference.The donation came through Reaching Out From Within, or ROFW, an incarcerated-led rehabilitation programme established in Kansas in 1982. According to the organisation, its purpose is to help incarcerated people make lasting changes in their behaviour, become role models for nonviolence and eventually return to their communities as contributing members. ROFW says its groups now operate in all 15 adult correctional facilities in Kansas, as well as facilities in North Carolina and a transition centre in Kansas City, Missouri. The programme uses regular meetings and peer support to encourage participants to examine destructive behaviour, develop healthier relationships and prepare for life after incarceration.The lunch-debt fundraiser also carried a personal connection for some of the men involved. Organisers said many participants had grown up in financially unstable households and remembered experiencing hunger themselves. That background gave the men a direct understanding of why a school meal can matter to a child whose family is struggling financially. The fundraiser therefore allowed participants to help children facing a problem that some of them had experienced earlier in their own lives. At the same time, the available reporting does not establish that every participant personally experienced childhood hunger, so that detail is best attributed to the organisers rather than applied to all of the men.The $4,267 contribution does not completely erase the district's reported $6,000 meal debt, but it substantially reduces it and provides direct assistance to families struggling with food costs. The episode has also prompted a broader conversation about food insecurity and the circumstances that allow school meal debt to accumulate in the first place. At the same time, the donation offers a striking example of the kind of community contribution that rehabilitation programmes such as ROFW seek to encourage. Men serving time at a Kansas correctional facility chose to use their own funds to help children outside its walls, turning a local financial problem into an opportunity for service and positive change.
Article Summary: Nearly 30 incarcerated men in northwest Kansas have donated $4,267 to help pay down unpaid school meal debt at Norton Community Schools. Members of Reaching Out From Within, a rehabilitation programme at Norton Correctional Facility, raised $3,810 from their personal funds during a spring and summer fundraiser. Kansas Department of Corrections staff added another $457, bringing the total to $ 4,267. The donation was presented to Norton Community schools Superintendent Corey Roy on August 3.

Article Title: 'Information sharing is through intelligence channels': Israel denies report UAE leader warned Netanyahu days before Oct 7 attack
Article Text:
Was Netanyahu warned in advance about Hamas attack?

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ’s office has rejected reports that he was warned in advance about the October 2023, Hamas attacks by UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed.In a post on X, the Israeli Prime Minister’s Office said any exchange of relevant information took place only through intelligence channels between the two countries.“The press reports are false. No warning was given to the Prime Minister by the United Arab Emirates before October 7. If there was any relevant information, it was passed through intelligence channels between the two countries,” it posted.According to a new investigative report published by Israeli newspaper Haaretz, Mohammed bin Zayed had warned Netanyahu that Hamas’ then-leader Yahya Sinwar was preparing a “major attack” on Israel.Netanyahu, however, did not share the warning with Israel’s senior security leadership.Around 10 days after their reported conversation, Hamas launched its attack on Israel on October 7, 2023.The Haaretz report is based on the new book "Kidnapped: 843 Days of Abandonment." It claimed that Mohammed bin Zayed spoke to Netanyahu for 45 minutes from Abu Dhabi.Bin Zayed also reportedly urged Netanyahu to address broader sources of instability, including Gaza’s economic situation and rising tensions in the West Bank.According to a UAE presidential advisor interviewed for the book, bin Zayed was “surprised” by Netanyahu’s response, as the Israeli prime minister did not appear “alarmed”.“He (Netanyahu) said that he believed Hamas was preparing to act in the West Bank and assured him that Israel was ready to respond to any scenario,” the report quoted the adviser as saying.The Emirati leader later discussed the warning with then-CIA Director William J Burns. Bin Zayed reportedly expressed concern that “something there is about to explode” and said Netanyahu had instead focused on the West Bank.Notwithstanding the clarification, the report is likely to pile further pressure on Netanyahu, who has repeatedly been accused of ignoring warning signs in the days leading up to the Hamas attack.The claims are also significant as they come ahead of the Israeli Knesset elections, scheduled for October 27, with Netanyahu seeking a seventh term in office.
Article Summary: UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed reportedly warned Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that Hamas was preparing a major attack. Israeli PM's office says any exchange of relevant information took place only through intelligence channels between the two countries. Report likely to pile further pressure on Netanyahu, who has repeatedly been accused of ignoring warning signs in the days leading up to the Hamas attack.

Article Title: Sheikh Hasina's daughter Saima Wazed resigns from WHO post following fraud allegations
Article Text:
Her departure comes amid allegations of financial fraud and misrepresentation of her academic credentials

Poll Vote & Share your view What should be the WHO's priority when handling allegations involving senior officials? Ensuring a fair investigation Maintaining transparency Protecting institutional credibility Following due process 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Saima Wazed, the World Health Organization’s Southeast Asia regional director and daughter of ousted Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina , has resigned from her post following fraud investigations by the UN agency and Bangladeshi authorities, Reuters reported on Wednesday.Wazed’s resignation was confirmed in a resignation letter seen by Reuters. Her departure comes amid allegations of financial fraud and misrepresentation of her academic credentials, which she has denied.The WHO placed Wazed on unpaid administrative leave after Bangladesh’s Anti-Corruption Commission filed cases against her in March 2025, alleging fraud, forgery and misuse of power. She was first sent on leave in July 2025.The WHO later accused Wazed of "committing financial fraud in relation to her travel to China" and of misrepresenting her academic credentials, according to a July 3, 2026, letter from her lawyers to the WHO seen by Reuters.Wazed’s removal from her WHO role had previously been welcomed by Bangladesh’s interim government as a step towards accountability. "We view this as an important first step toward accountability," then-chief adviser’s press secretary Shafiqul Alam had said in 2025."We firmly believe that a permanent resolution is necessary, one that removes Saima from her position, revokes all associated privileges and restores integrity to this prestigious role and the credibility of the UN system as a whole," he had said.The development comes as Bangladesh continues to seek the extradition of Hasina and other Awami League leaders from India. New Delhi has said the request is being "examined as part of our established processes".
Article Summary: Saima Wazed, the World Health Organization’s Southeast Asia regional director and daughter of ousted Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, has resigned from her post. Her departure comes amid allegations of financial fraud and misrepresentation of her academic credentials, which she has denied.

Article Title: 'Make ground in Gaza tremble': Egypt warned Netanyahu of Hamas plans before October 7
Article Text:
Details emerge on Egypt’s warning to Netanyahu

Fresh details have emerged about warnings issued to Israel ahead of the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack, amid a report that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was warned by the United Arab Emirates about plans for a major assault in the weeks leading up to the invasion.The latest information also sheds further light on previously reported warnings from Egyptian intelligence officials during the same period.According to Army Radio, the Shin Bet intelligence service conveyed to Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu warnings from its Egyptian counterparts that Hamas intended to “make the ground in Gaza tremble.”The Egyptian side provided only a general warning, without offering any specific details.In the days following the October 7 onslaught, an Egyptian intelligence official said Jerusalem had ignored repeated warnings that the Gaza-based terror group was planning “something big,” including an apparent direct warning from Cairo’s intelligence minister to Netanyahu, as cited by Times of Israel.According to the report, then-Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar assessed that the warning referred, at least in part, to Hamas seeking to raise the issue of kidnapped Israeli researcher Elizabeth Tsurkov in talks with Israel over a potential hostage deal.Shortly before the warning was issued, Hamas and Iraqi Shiite militia Kataeb Hezbollah, the group holding Tsurkov, had reportedly agreed that she would be treated as a Hamas asset in negotiations with Israel.The talks would involve the release of a large number of terrorists in exchange for the handover of two Israeli captives and the bodies of two IDF soldiers held in Gaza.The development comes as a new investigative report by Israeli newspaper Haaretz claimed that UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed had warned Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that then-Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was preparing a “major attack” against Israel. Netanyahu, however, reportedly did not share the warning with Israel’s senior security leadership.Around 10 days after their reported conversation, Hamas launched its October 7, 2023, attack on Israel.The Haaretz report is based on the new book Kidnapped: 843 Days of Abandonment, which claims that bin Zayed spoke to Netanyahu for 45 minutes from Abu Dhabi. During the conversation, bin Zayed also reportedly urged Netanyahu to address broader sources of instability, including Gaza’s economic situation and rising tensions in the West Bank.According to a UAE presidential adviser interviewed for the book, bin Zayed was “surprised” by Netanyahu’s response, saying the Israeli prime minister did not appear “alarmed”.However, Netanyahu's office has rejected the claims made by the report.In a post on X, the Israeli Prime Minister’s Office said that any exchange of relevant information between the two countries took place solely through intelligence channels.“The press reports are false. No warning was given to the Prime Minister by the United Arab Emirates before October 7. If there was any relevant information, it was passed through intelligence channels between the two countries,” it posted.
Article Summary: Details emerge about warnings issued to Israel ahead of October 7, 2023, Hamas attack. Israel's Shin Bet intelligence service warned that Hamas intended to ‘make the ground in Gaza tremble’ Egyptian intelligence official said Jerusalem had ignored repeated warnings that the Gaza-based terror group was planning ‘something big’

Article Title: In 1951, an artist and a librarian built a riverside cabin with no electricity and lived from the land for 35 years; their 61-acre homestead is now being preserved
Article Text:
The preservation effort entered a new phase in 2022, when a nonprofit organization named Payne Hollow in Ohio acquired the 61-acre property | instagram/@paynehollowontheohio

The 61-acre Payne Hollow property went to Paul Hassfurder, an artist who had become a close friend of the Hubbards | instagram/@paynehollowontheohio

They built a life around the river

The property passed to a caretaker

The preservation effort entered a new phase in 2022, when a nonprofit organization named Payne Hollow in Ohio acquired the 61-acre property | instagram/@paynehollowontheohio

A nonprofit took over the 61 acres

Harlan and Anna Hubbard settled beside the Ohio River in Kentucky in 1951 after traveling by shantyboat for years. The following year, they began building the small cabin that became Payne Hollow, which is a home where they lived with few modern conveniences and relied heavily on the surrounding land and river.Harlan Hubbard was an artist, writer and craftsman, and Anna was a librarian and musician. Together they developed a life around the property in Trimble County, Kentucky, and grew food, gathered wood and made much of what they needed themselves. Historical records place the cabin’s construction in 1952, after the Hubbards had negotiated for land at Payne's Landing. A University of Louisville-related historical account says they returned to the site in May 1952, arranged to rent and later purchase seven acres, and moved into a one-room cabin by November that year. The structure expanded into a two-room home in 1954.The Hubbards built their shantyboat in 1944 and traveled along the Ohio and Mississippi river system before settling at the Kentucky site, and at Payne Hollow, the couple continued the same basic approach to daily life. Hanover College's account of the property says that they rejected modern conveniences and lived without electricity or running water, while relying on the land around their home.Harlan painted, wrote and produced woodcuts, and often used materials and subjects connected to the Ohio River landscape. He is credited with more than 1,000 works of art. Anna was a librarian and musician, and the couple's life included music as well as Harlan's painting and writing. They remained at Payne Hollow for more than three decades. Anna died in 1986, while Harlan died in 1988. By then, the property had become closely associated with their work and the self-sufficient life they had created there. Hanover College says the couple's riverside property eventually encompassed 61 acres, including the buildings and their contents.The 61-acre Payne Hollow property went to Paul Hassfurder, an artist who had become a close friend of the Hubbards and helped them during their later years, after Harlan's death. Hassfurder moved into the house shortly after Harlan died and continued living there in much the same spirit as the couple. Earlier accounts of Payne Hollow describe him maintaining the property and resisting major changes that could have altered its character.Payne Hollow sits along the Ohio River in Trimble County, downstream from Madison, Indiana, and access has historically involved the river and a wooded route rather than the kind of infrastructure that is associated with conventional residential development. The property remained closely associated with Hubbard's artwork and writing, while concerns about the condition of its buildings grew. Preservationists were already discussing ways to protect the house, studio and surrounding land by the 2000s.The preservation effort entered a new phase in 2022, when a nonprofit organization named Payne Hollow in Ohio acquired the 61-acre property. The organization was established to preserve the land and structures and to develop educational and research uses around the Hubbard legacy. Hanover College reported that the group planned to stabilize the buildings, safeguard historically significant artifacts and conduct ecological work on the property.The organization has described the site as a work in progress, and its own account says the house and studio are deteriorating and need restoration, while recent photographs document the property as it exists today. The organization is also documenting the surrounding land, trails and ecological features while developing plans for future stewardship.When Hanover College reported on the acquisition in 2022, Payne Hollow was closed to the public while the nonprofit developed its preservation and access plans. The property had moved from private inheritance into the hands of an organization specifically created to maintain the land, buildings and collection that were associated with Harlan and Anna Hubbard.
Article Summary: Harlan and Anna Hubbard settled beside the Ohio River in Kentucky in 1951 after traveling by shantyboat for years. The following year, they began building the small cabin that became Payne Hollow, which is a home where they lived with few modern conveniences and relied heavily on the surrounding land and river. In 2022, a nonprofit organization named Payne Hollow in Ohio acquired the 61-acre property.

Article Title: In 1999, James Cameron bought a 102-acre California ranch for $4.4 million. 24 years later, the $33 million estate revealed a life far beyond Hollywood
Article Text:
Inside James Cameron’s 102-acre California coastal ranch

The ranch that became Cameron’s private workshop

PC: Forbes

The ranch was built to produce its own power, water and food

A childhood shaped by animals, beaches and open space

The $33 million sale goes far beyond the main house

The Gaviota Coast remains unusually undeveloped

Why the Camerons decided to sell

A $4.375 million purchase became a $33 million asking price

James Cameron bought his 102-acre California ranch in 1999 for about $4.4 million, creating a private retreat far removed from Hollywood's usual celebrity lifestyle. Set within the secluded Hollister Ranch on Santa Barbara County's Gaviota Coast, the property became a family home, writing retreat, working farm and base for the filmmaker's interest in deep-sea exploration and robotics. Over the next two decades, Cameron and his family transformed the estate while preserving its rural character, adding extensive gardens, renewable energy systems, animal facilities and specialised workspaces. When the ranch was listed for $33 million in 2023, its value reflected not just the house, but the unusual life built across its 102 acres.According to a Forbes report, the property sits inside Hollister Ranch, a large private coastal community in Santa Barbara County established in 1971. The wider ranch covers about 14,400 acres, with roughly 8.5 miles of coastline and 136 parcels. Development has remained tightly controlled, with each parcel generally spanning around 100 acres and only a small portion available for residential construction.The main house, built in the 1980s by Hollister Ranch builder Bob Curtis, had about 8,000 square feet of living space when the couple bought it. “It feels rural, but it’s also quite bold, architecturally.It’s very comfortable. It’s not precious,” said James.The interiors reflected the couple's taste for Balinese and Indonesian furnishings. The primary bedroom, for instance, incorporated Balinese fabric and oak flooring, while the great room contained an enormous stone head of Dionysus that Cameron said had come from the façade of a New York hotel.The ranch was not simply somewhere the filmmaker went between productions. It became a place where some of his writing took shape.Cameron used the upper library in the main house as a retreat while working on the scripts for Avatar and later films in the series. A separate 2,000-square-foot guest house, positioned higher on the property, also gave him a secluded place to work.For long stretches, he could simply disappear from the usual demands of film production. The isolation suited the kind of concentrated writing he needed to do, particularly as the Avatar projects expanded into multiple films.The property's connection to Cameron's work extended beyond screenwriting. One of the ranch's two barns became a practical workspace for his interest in deep-sea exploration and robotics. The larger barn measures about 24,000 square feet. Cameron said he had kept helicopters there and used the building while developing submarines and robotic equipment for expeditions. Those projects included his extensive work connected with the wreck of the Titanic and his 2012 solo descent into the Mariana Trench.The house was designed for family life, while the surrounding buildings could accommodate equipment associated with some of Cameron's more technically demanding projects.There was also a practical side to the couple's approach to the ranch. The property was equipped to operate off-grid, using solar and wind power. Cameron said the system had extensive battery storage and was capable of supporting the property's roughly 100-kilowatt system for extended periods.Water and food were part of the same arrangement. A well supplied irrigation, while domestic water came through the Santa Anita Mutual Water Company. The garden covered about three-quarters of an acre and contained roughly 150 different crops.It was large enough to become a genuine source of food rather than simply an ornamental garden. Cameron estimated that it could provide produce for 40 or 50 people, with the home's pantry offering further storage.The garden also reflected the family's approach to food and agriculture. The Camerons adopted a plant-based diet in 2012 and had developed broader interests in agricultural and environmental practices elsewhere, including farming operations in New Zealand and Saskatchewan.For more than two decades, the ranch was also where the Cameron children grew up.The scale of the property meant that childhood there looked rather different from life in a conventional suburban house. There were horses, donkeys, goats and a pig. The children went hiking, explored the coastline and learned about the animals and plants around them.The family could check tide tables, walk down to the beach and explore the coastal environment without having to leave the ranch's wider surroundings. Some of the stories from those years were less predictable. Cameron recalled the children bringing home animals they encountered, including a young bobcat that the family named Rex. After being raised and eventually released into the wild, the bobcat later returned to the area. It also killed the family's turkey.The ranch was large enough to accommodate gatherings, too. Around the time the property was listed, the Camerons had hosted a five-day family reunion involving about 30 relatives.The residence represents only part of what was being offered for $33 million. The property includes an equestrian facility of about 4,795 square feet, complete with paddocks and ranch offices. Caretaker accommodation and four apartments are incorporated into the ranch facilities.There are also two barns, along with a tennis court and a permitted helipad. The arrangement is significant because the land was never simply carved out as a luxury residential compound. Hollister Ranch has retained its agricultural identity, with cattle ranching continuing across much of the broader property.That working landscape sits alongside the coastal setting. From inside the Cameron house, large windows look towards the bluffs and the Pacific. San Miguel Island, the westernmost of California's Channel Islands, can be seen across the water.Whales, dolphins and sea otters are among the wildlife visible from the property.The ranch's value is tied not only to what has been built on it but also to what surrounds it.The Gaviota Coast stretches for about 76 miles along Santa Barbara County and contains one of Southern California's largest remaining stretches of undeveloped coastline. Its landscape brings together coastal bluffs, grasslands, scrub, estuaries and intertidal environments.The area also forms part of a wider ecological corridor associated with the Channel Islands. Development along this section of coast has remained comparatively limited, which gives large private parcels a very different character from the more heavily built-up coastal areas farther south.Hollister Ranch itself has a long history of cattle ranching. The land was established as a private community while retaining much of its agricultural landscape, and residents have access to sections of the shoreline.For the Camerons, the natural setting was closely tied to the way the property was used. It was somewhere to work and raise a family, but also somewhere where the surrounding landscape was part of ordinary life.The decision to list the ranch in 2023 was not presented as a response to a problem with the property. By then, their three children were largely living independently. Cameron's professional commitments had also become spread across several locations. His work on Avatar took him between Los Angeles and Wellington, New Zealand, while upcoming Alita: Battle Angel projects were expected to take him to Austin.Maintaining a large coastal ranch made less practical sense when the family was no longer based there in the same way. The couple said they hoped a future owner with young children might make similar use of the property.The Camerons paid $4.375 million for the ranch in 1999. Twenty-four years later, the asking price had reached $33 million. That represents an increase of $28.625 million in the property's nominal value. Put another way, the 2023 asking price was roughly 7.5 times what the couple paid.The increase cannot simply be attributed to changes made to the house. The property sits in a highly restricted coastal setting where large parcels are scarce, and comparable sales within Hollister Ranch have commanded substantial prices. Around the time Cameron's property was listed, another front-row Hollister Ranch parcel reportedly sold off-market for $32.5 million, setting a then-record price for the community.
Article Summary: James Cameron bought his 102-acre California ranch in 1999 for about $4.4 million. The property became a family home, writing retreat, working farm and base for the filmmaker's interest in deep-sea exploration and robotics. The main house was designed for family life, while the surrounding buildings could accommodate equipment associated with some of Cameron's more technically demanding projects.

Article Title: In 1912, a young homesteader walked deep into British Columbia’s mountains and spent 54 years at an isolated lake; his family helped save its trumpeter swans, and the homestead eventually joined a pro
Article Text:
Ralph Edwards (LEFT), Trumpeter swans (RIGHT): Wikimedia Commons

Ralph Edwards (LEFT), Trumpeter swans (RIGHT): Wikimedia Commons

The lake became a refuge for swans

Crusoe of Lonesome Lake

Edwards built a life far from the nearest settlement

Image of the Rainbow Range in Tweedsmuir South Provincial Park | Wikimedia Commons

The homestead eventually became a conservation project

Ralph Edwards was looking for a place where he could build a homestead that was surrounded by mountains, and first reached Lonesome Lake in British Columbia in the winter of 1912. The nearest settlement was roughly 40 miles away, and Edwards spent his first years there largely on his own. He eventually built a home, established a farm and married Ethel Hober, who joined him in the wilderness. Their three children grew up at Lonesome Lake, where the family also became closely involved with the survival of the trumpeter swan. Edwards remained at Lonesome Lake until 1966, which gave him more than five decades there. The place that began as his remote homestead is now part of the landscape of Tweedsmuir Provincial Park.Trumpeter swans were under severe pressure from hunting upon Edwards’ arrival. The species had been heavily hunted for its feathers and meat, and only about 100 birds were estimated to remain in North America in the early 20th century. Lonesome Lake was one of the places where a small wintering flock survived, and a 2021 account of the conservation effort published by Post Alley says that roughly 30 trumpeter swans wintered there when the Edwards family became involved.The family began feeding the birds during difficult winters, and eventually worked with the Canadian Wildlife Service.The wintering flock at Lonesome Lake had grown to about 600 birds by the 1960s, according to Post Alley. The feeding was not a casual task, as corn had to be transported into the remote valley, often by packhorse. Members of the Edwards family took turns to maintain the supply through winter, when natural food could become scarce. The Edwards family became known for their work with the species, and Ralph Edwards was later portrayed in Leland Stowe's book The BC Parks Foundation says that Edwards received a 153-acre tract at Lonesome Lake in 1913 through a homesteading program, about a year after he first reached the lake. He spent the next decade clearing land and building a home and rarely left the property. He returned after serving in the First World War, married Ethel and raised their three children there.Lonesome Lake lies in the Atnarko-Kliniklini trench system in the Coast Mountains, southeast of Bella Coola, and the BC Parks Foundation describes the property as being about 69 kilometres southeast of Bella Coola and surrounded by the wilderness of Tweedsmuir Provincial Park. British Columbia's official geographical names database says that Edwards named the lake Lonesome Lake after arriving there in the winter of 1912 and finding no other living creatures in sight. The same record credits Ralph and Ethel Edwards with doing more to protect trumpeter swans from extinction than anyone else.Edwards left Lonesome Lake in 1966, and the property remained in the family. But the original homestead buildings did not survive, when a forest fire destroyed the Edwards family's farm buildings in 2004. A later account of the property noted that the land was gradually reverting to wilderness, even as the family's role in the recovery of trumpeter swans remained attached to the site.The old homestead was a privately owned parcel surrounded by provincial parkland, and was effectively an inholding inside Tweedsmuir Provincial Park. The BC Parks Foundation launched a campaign to acquire it rather than allow it to be sold for private development. The organization described the land as an important piece of both conservation history and the wider wilderness of Tweedsmuir.In 2021, the campaign reached its target, when a postscript that was added to the Post Alley account reported that the foundation had raised C$700,000 and purchased the Lonesome Lake homestead from Edwards' descendants, with the intention of making it part of the park. The BC Parks Foundation now lists the protected property at 62 hectares, or about 153 acres. It says the MapleCross Fund helped the foundation protect the former Edwards homestead in 2020 and describes the property as a private inholding that was brought into public park ownership. The original house is gone, but the lake and the conservation history that was associated with the Edwards family remain within Tweedsmuir's protected landscape.
Article Summary: Ralph Edwards first reached Lonesome Lake in British Columbia in the winter of 1912. The nearest settlement was roughly 40 miles away, and Edwards spent his first years there largely on his own. He eventually built a home, established a farm and married Ethel Hober, who joined him in the wilderness. Their three children grew up at the lake, where the family became closely involved with the survival of the trumpeter swan.

Article Title: In 1895, a naturalist built a bark-covered cabin in the New York woods to escape visitors and write in solitude; after his death, it became the heart of a 170-acre wildlife sanctuary
Article Text:
Burroughs built Slabsides in 1895 | Wikimedia Commons

Burroughs built Slabsides in 1895 | Wikimedia Commons

The cabin was built as an escape

Nine acres became 170

Burroughs poses with Thomas Edison and Henry Ford at Edison's home in Ft. Myers, Florida, 1914 | Wikimedia Commons

Slabsides remains largely intact

John Burroughs had become popular enough by 1895, and visitors were disrupting the quiet he needed to write. His answer was a small cabin in the woods near his West Park, New York, home. Burroughs built Slabsides that year with help from his son and a carpenter, and used rough wooden slabs with their bark still attached for the exterior walls. The cabin sat on a wooded tract about a mile from Riverby, which was the home where Burroughs lived with his family. The naturalist used the retreat for writing, farming and observation, and it eventually became the physical center of a much larger nature sanctuary that now covers about 170 acres.Burroughs was already an established nature writer when Slabsides went up, with his books having made him one of the best-known American writers on the natural world, and the attention brought visitors to Riverby. The Hudson River Valley Institute 's historical account says Slabsides served several purposes, but one was to give Burroughs a place away from the steady stream of people arriving at Riverby. He also used the property for farming, cultivating celery in a reclaimed swamp beside the cabin.The name came from the cabin's construction, and its outside walls were covered with rough slabs of wood that still carried their bark. Inside, it had an open main room, a partitioned sleeping area and a fireplace. Burroughs made some of the furniture himself, and much of the interior has survived.Visitors of the cabin included naturalist John Muir, President Theodore Roosevelt and industrialist Henry Ford. Burroughs wrote several works at Slabsides, and used the surrounding woods as both a workplace and a source of material for his nature writing.Burroughs and his son developed about nine acres around the cabin, and after Burroughs died in 1921, the property passed to the John Burroughs Association, which had been established to preserve his work and legacy. Supporters raised money to acquire additional parcels as logging and development threatened nearby woodland in the 1960s.Today, the John Burroughs Sanctuary encompasses about 170 acres, with Slabsides at its center. The surrounding property contains woodland and hiking trails rather than the development that Burroughs had sought to avoid when he first built the cabin. The cabin itself received federal recognition in 1968, when it was designated a National Historic Landmark. The landscape is now maintained for both conservation and public access, and the sanctuary grounds are open year-round, while access to the cabin is more limited. The Library of Congress holds photographs of Burroughs at Riverby and Slabsides that were taken between 1915 and 1922. Its catalog says the collection includes images of the naturalist, his family and visitors at the cabin and lists the photographs as having no known restrictions on publication.The sanctuary's trails run through the woods that Burroughs used for walking and observation, while the cabin preserves the setting in which he wrote. The additional acreage was acquired specifically to keep the woods around the cabin from being broken up as development expanded, which makes the 170-acre sanctuary considerably different from the nine-acre tract on which Burroughs originally built his retreat. The property is still maintained by the John Burroughs Association, and is available for hiking, while the cabin is opened on selected occasions and special tours rather than operating as a conventional daily museum.
Article Summary: John Burroughs built Slabsides in 1895 as an escape from visitors to his home in West Park, New York. The naturalist used the retreat for writing, farming and observation, and it eventually became the physical center of a much larger nature sanctuary that now covers about 170 acres. The cabin received federal recognition in 1968, when it was designated a National Historic Landmark.

Article Title: In 2019, Seattle residents helped float planted “biobarges” beside a hardened waterway; cameras later recorded young salmon feeding around the new habitat
Article Text:
AI Representation: Urban upcycling supports salmon in Seattle. Image credits: Chatgpt

Four

biobarges

, each holding four planted biofilters, were deployed

The biobarges were towed into place at two Duwamish sites in April 2019

Coleman NFH Chinook salmon juvenile in raceway. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Underwater footage shows salmon using the structures

According to NOAA's Lower Duwamish River hazardous-waste site summary, the river once had extensive tidal marshes and mudflats along its banks before channelization and filling transformed much of the estuary into an industrial waterway. Dredging, channeling and a century of industrial activity have destroyed 97 percent of the tidal wetlands that once lined the riverbanks, according to a University of Washington-led study on the Duwamish Floating Wetlands Project. According to the project background for the Duwamish Floating Wetlands Project, along the first seven miles of the Duwamish River, 40 to 60 percent of the linear shoreline is bulkhead, and 50 to 80 percent is riprap. That hardened shoreline leaves young salmon migrating from fresh to salt water with little cover from predators or access to food.The team of scientists, headed by Green Futures Lab in collaboration with the Port of Seattle, King County and volunteers from the community, designed four platforms known as Biobarges that were used during a two-year pilot and not as a permanent installation. Each biobarge held four floating wetlands, called Biofilters, planted with native species sturdy enough for scientists to take measurements from.In April 2019, Biobarges were launched into the river and placed within the Duwamish Estuary at two sites. Two of the biobarges were positioned at a heavily industrialized site downriver, while the other two were placed farther upriver in a more vegetated stretch of the river, allowing researchers to compare fish use across a hardened site and a more natural one, according to a University of Washington graduate student's account in the SMEA Currents blog . Monitoring continued through the out-migration season and ran until July 2019, marking the first year of a two-year proof-of-concept pilot project. The structures were then monitored again in 2020, according to the Green Futures Lab website.Local volunteers trained as community scientists carried out much of the fieldwork. They counted and identified juvenile salmon near the Biobarges and at separate reference and control sites without floating wetlands. They also set up and collected the GoPro cameras that recorded underwater footage at each structure. In the project's second year, the volunteers reviewed hundreds of hours of video to identify and count the fish captured on camera, as documented in the study.The rationale for the concept is pretty straightforward. The Green Futures Lab's project background page notes that out-migrating juvenile salmonids rely on a diet of benthic aquatic invertebrates, such as nereid worms and gammarid amphipods, and terrestrial invertebrates, including chironomids, aphids, and tethinids, which are typically produced by vegetation in healthy tidal marshes. Because the bank is reinforced with riprap and lacks vegetation, the Biofilters are intended to attract those insects and invertebrates.Indeed, the footage taken by the GoPro cameras shows juvenile fish, particularly Chinook, swimming around the Biobarges rather than avoiding them. This early observation hints that the floating platforms may be functioning as intended, offering fish a place to linger and feed in a stretch of river where hardened banks and the loss of natural shoreline otherwise limit such opportunities, though the project describes itself as a proof-of-concept pilot rather than a confirmed result. Seattle residents did more than watch the project; they helped assemble the platforms, plant vegetation and observe fish behavior. In fact, they helped put together the platforms, plant vegetation and observe fish behavior.
Article Summary: The Duwamish River once had extensive tidal marshes and mudflats along its banks before channelization and filling transformed much of the estuary into an industrial waterway. Dredging, channeling and a century of industrial activity have destroyed 97 percent of the tidal wetlands that once lined the riverbanks. Scientists designed four platforms known as Biobarges that were used during a two-year pilot.

Article Title: US states sue Trump administration, accuse it of ‘illegally’ weakening wildlife law
Article Text:
The Endangered Species Act, enacted by Congress in 1973, has been credited with helping save species including the California condor, grizzly bear and humpback whale. The states said 99% of the species protected under the law have avoided extinction.

Twenty US states and Washington, DC, sued US President Donald Trump's administration on Wednesday, challenging new rules that they say weaken the federal Endangered Species Act. They said that the rules could allow development, mining and oil drilling in habitats of threatened wildlife.The lawsuits, led by Washington state, California, Maryland and Massachusetts, were filed in federal courts in the San Francisco area. They target rules issued by the interior and commerce departments less than two months ago that changed how the landmark 1973 law protects endangered species and their habitats.One lawsuit challenges a new definition of "harm" under the Endangered Species Act. The states say the change removes long-standing protections for wildlife habitats by allowing activities such as oil drilling and mining as long as they are not "directed immediately and intentionally" against particular animals, even if they result in injury or death.The states called the change a "reversal of staggering proportions".They argue that the rules are "arbitrary and capricious" and violate the National Environmental Policy Act.The second lawsuit challenges two other changes. One removes broad protections for species newly classified as threatened unless the US Fish and Wildlife Service introduces protections specifically for that species. The other requires the government to consider objections from businesses, including potential economic costs, before designating areas as "critical habitats".Washington attorney general Nick Brown said the administration was weakening a law that has protected wildlife for decades."The ‌Trump administration is trying to undermine the law, the will of Congress and the will of the people who overwhelmingly support protections ​for endangered species," Washington attorney General ​Nick Brown said at a press conference. "Instead of stewardship, this administration's approach to our land, to our water is one of exploitation."The US interior department rejected the states' claims and said federal agencies should implement the law according to its text."The role of federal agencies is to faithfully implement the Endangered Species Act as written, not to expand its reach through interpretations favoured by advocacy organisations," an Interior Department spokesperson said."This lawsuit seeks to preserve a decades-old regulatory overreach that expanded the Endangered Species Act beyond the authority granted by Congress," the spokesperson added. "The department will vigorously defend its authority to implement the law according to its plain text."The Endangered Species Act, enacted by Congress in 1973, has been credited with helping save species including the California condor, grizzly bear and humpback whale. The states said 99% of the species protected under the law have avoided extinction.Wildlife advocates have long identified habitat loss as a major cause of extinction. New York attorney general Letitia James said the states were seeking to preserve protections for future generations."We owe future generations a world where bald eagles soar, sea turtles ​swim and all wildlife thrives," New York Attorney General Letitia James said in a statement.The Trump administration has argued that the law has been used to block development projects and impose costs on businesses. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has said the Endangered Species Act has been weaponised to stop projects, hurt competitiveness and undermine national security.Burgum has said the new rules bring the law closer to its original intent.The changes come as the Trump administration seeks to reduce environmental regulations that it says constrain American businesses. The administration has also rolled back several environmental initiatives and reduced support for clean energy.The new rules followed a 2024 US Supreme Court decision that overturned a decades-old precedent requiring courts to defer to federal agencies' reasonable interpretations of laws they administer.The latest lawsuits add to dozens of legal challenges filed by Democratic-led states against major policy changes during Trump's second term. Environmental groups have separately sued to block the revised definition of "harm".
Article Summary: Twenty US states and Washington, DC, sued US President Donald Trump's administration on Wednesday. They say new rules could allow development, mining and oil drilling in habitats of threatened wildlife. One lawsuit challenges a new definition of "harm" under the Endangered Species Act.

Article Title: A car crash left this Army veteran paralysed; seven years later, he graduated with a petroleum engineering degree
Article Text:
Rocky Fernandez’s life changed after a car crash left him paralysed

VA support helped Fernandez stay focused on college

PC: US Department of Veterans Affairs

His recovery extended beyond medical treatment

Fernandez’s recovery has also inspired him to help other veterans

After years of setbacks, Fernandez finally earned his degree

Rocky Fernandez’s life took an unexpected turn when a car crash left the Army veteran paralysed, forcing him to rebuild plans that had once seemed straightforward. Recovery brought hospital stays, rehabilitation and medical setbacks, but his ambitions did not disappear. As reported by the US Department of Veterans Affairs, with support from the Houston VA and vocational services, Fernandez returned to education and worked towards a petroleum engineering degree. Seven years after the accident, he reached a milestone that once seemed difficult to imagine: graduation. His journey involved far more than completing coursework, requiring him to balance ongoing health challenges with college and daily life. Now, he is preparing to begin a career in petroleum engineering.Before the crash, Fernandez was an Army veteran with plans that centred on education and what might come afterwards. The accident altered those plans almost immediately.The years that followed were marked by medical complications and rehabilitation. There were extended periods in hospital, including treatment for a serious infection, while adapting to life with paralysis brought a different set of demands outside the hospital as well.Going back to college was therefore not simply a matter of returning to a classroom. Fernandez had to work around circumstances that could make attending classes, studying and managing everyday tasks considerably more complicated.Reportedly, he found support at the Michael E. DeBakey VA Medical Center in Houston, where treatment was accompanied by services aimed at helping him regain some independence and continue pursuing his education.Vocational support became an important part of that process.
