Shaun Smith, Fernandez’s vocational counsellor at the VA, helped him work through some of the obstacles between his circumstances and his college plans.For Fernandez, that assistance formed part of a much larger effort. Medical care, rehabilitation and practical support all had to fit around the same goal: getting his education finished.His vocational counselor Shaun Smith said Fernandez's approach was striking because he remained focused on what he wanted to achieve rather than allowing each setback to change the destination.“I’m not gonna lie, it was hard to have faith after all these setbacks,” Fernandez said. He eventually learned to slow things down, deal with what was in front of him and keep moving.Fernandez has also become a regular presence at the Houston VA's wellness programmes. Among the activities he attends is weekly yoga, where he works with yoga therapist Darcy Robinson.His sessions have included meditation, deep relaxation and sound-bowl therapy alongside yoga. Robinson described Fernandez as willing to experiment with different approaches to his wellbeing, rather than treating rehabilitation as something confined to conventional medical appointments.For staff who have worked with Fernandez, these activities have offered another view of his recovery. He is not only someone receiving care. He has also become familiar to people around the medical centre, where his regular presence and interactions with staff have made him a recognisable figure.Dr Donna Huang, one of the physicians involved in his care, said Fernandez continued to think about other veterans even while dealing with his own complicated medical course. During the early stages of rehabilitation, he was already considering how he might eventually support people facing spinal cord injuries themselves.Fernandez came to view disability as part of the range of human experience rather than something that should determine what a person can or cannot attempt. He hoped to become a peer support partner for veterans dealing with similar injuries.Huang said, “What stood out about taking care of Rocky was his unwavering resilience and optimism in the face of a complicated medical course with multiple setbacks.”Fernandez now puts that idea into simpler terms. He believes there are fewer fixed boundaries around what a person can accomplish than circumstances might initially suggest.The graduation this spring marked the completion of a course of study that began before his accident and continued through years of profound change.Fernandez now has a petroleum engineering degree from Houston City College. The qualification does not erase the medical complications or the limitations he still lives with. It does, however, give him something concrete to build on after a period in which much of his life had to be reorganised around recovery.His next step is already taking shape. He is looking for work in petroleum engineering and wants to use the degree he worked so long to obtain.
Article Summary: Rocky Fernandez was paralysed in a car crash seven years ago. With support from the US Department of Veterans Affairs and vocational services, he returned to education and worked towards a petroleum engineering degree. Now, he is preparing to begin a career in petroleum engineering.

Article Title: Why Trump's flight to Dallas was delayed before republican midterm convention
Article Text:
President Donald Trump talks with reporters after an emergency inflatable slide deployed on Air Force One before before Trump arrived to board at Joint Base Andrews, Md., Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026. (AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin)

US President Donald Trump’s flight to Dallas was briefly delayed on Wednesday after an emergency inflatable slide deployed from Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews.Trump was headed to Dallas for the republican midterm convention to deliver the keynote address on Wednesday night.He told the reporters that the personnel were checking the emergency slide.“They’re checking the slide over here. And I think it's gonna take 15 minutes,” Trump said, adding that the aircraft was safe to fly.A person briefed on the situation told ABC News that military personnel had accidentally triggered the slide.When asked why the slide was being checked and whether there was a security concern, Trump said personnel wanted to make sure it “works perfectly”.Emergency slides are not typically checked by deploying them before departure because removing and replacing them is a time-consuming process.The slide was later removed from the aircraft and hauled away on the back of a pick-up truck before the plane took off for Dallas. Trump’s previous Air Force One was also brought out as a backup option.The newly modified aircraft, a gift from the Qatari royal family worth $400 million, has faced questions from some lawmakers and ethics experts over the unprecedented foreign gift.Trump had earlier described the approximately 14-year-old aircraft as “the world's most luxurious plane”. In July, he said the plane would be “maxed out”, with the process expected to take about a month.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump’s flight to Dallas was briefly delayed on Wednesday after an emergency inflatable slide deployed from Air Force One. Trump was headed to Dallas for the republican midterm convention to deliver the keynote address on Wednesday night. A person briefed on the situation said military personnel had accidentally triggered the slide.

Article Title: Plane crashes on San Diego runway, 2 killed; footage shows massive fire
Article Text:
The plane crashed and burst into flames while attempting to land at Montgomery-Gibbs Executive Airport in San Diego

Two people were killed after a Cessna Skyhawk plane crashed and burst into flames while attempting to land at Montgomery-Gibbs Executive Airport in San Diego on Monday.Footage recorded after the crash shows the small white plane sitting on the airport taxiway with a severe fire concentrated around the aircraft’s rear area, with flames producing a dense plume of black smoke that stretches across the taxiway.The aircraft itself appears to remain largely intact, while the area around the rear of the plane is heavily engulfed in flames.The aircraft reportedly plunged into the runway at the airport, with eyewitnesses capturing footage of the crash and the intense fire that followed. Witnesses said the flames were so severe that they could not get close to the aircraft.Mauricio Godinez and Melizza Cardiel Godinez were at a nearby hangar when they heard the plane hit the runway. Speaking to ABC 10, Godinez recalled: “We heard this loud boom. She peeks out, she tells me a plane crashed”.“I peek outside, and yes, a plane definitely crashed”.Cardiel said the intensity of the fire prevented them from approaching the aircraft.“The flames was just too much”, Cardiel recalled.“If we would have gotten in there, we would have gotten burned ourselves.”Investigators from the national transportation safety board and the federal aviation administration examined the crash site on Tuesday to determine what caused the accident, according to the New York Post.An initial FAA report said the aircraft crashed while the pilot was attempting to land. The plane's left wing dipped before it “appeared to stall and spun into the ground”, according to the report obtained by ABC 10.Surveillance footage from earlier showed the aircraft appearing to gain elevation before suddenly diving towards the ground at the airport early Monday evening, ABC 10 reported.The identities of the two people killed in the crash have not yet been released.The crash occurred two days after another plane crash in Fresno that killed all four people on board.
Article Summary: Two people were killed after a Cessna Skyhawk plane crashed and burst into flames while attempting to land at Montgomery-Gibbs Executive Airport in San Diego. Witnesses said the flames were so severe that they could not get close to the aircraft. The identities of the two people killed in the crash have not yet been released.

Article Title: For years, plastic bags were treated as waste; then one Nebraska city tried turning 2 million of them into a road
Article Text:
A 4,000-foot road section becomes Nebraska’s first plastic-bag pavement

Turning discarded bags into road material

The experiment moved from an overseas idea to a Nebraska road

The road offers plastic bags a second life inside the pavement

A road in South Sioux City, Nebraska, looks much like any other stretch of asphalt from behind the wheel. Beneath its surface, though, is material that would normally have had a very different fate. In June 2025, crews paved about 4,000 feet of Foundry Road using an asphalt mixture containing shredded plastic bags. Roughly two million bags were processed for the project, turning lightweight waste into part of a working road. The experiment is Nebraska’s first of its kind and is being watched as a practical test of whether discarded plastic can find a useful place in infrastructure. For now, the pavement is doing something ordinary: carrying traffic while an unusual idea is put to the test.According to Nebraska Public Media, construction crews laid the material on Foundry Road in June 2025. Shredded plastic bags were incorporated into the asphalt mixture alongside conventional road-building materials before the paving work began.For anyone driving over the completed stretch, there is no obvious visual difference. The plastic is not sitting on the surface or forming a separate layer. It has been processed and incorporated into the paving material.The project covered roughly 4,000 feet of road, making it a relatively small-scale test rather than a citywide change to road construction. Its purpose was to put the approach into practice and provide an opportunity to see how the resulting pavement performs.Plastic shopping and carrier bags can be awkward to recycle through ordinary systems. They are lightweight, easily blown away and can become mixed with other waste. In South Sioux City, the project offered a different destination for some of that material.About two million recycled bags were shredded for the road. Once processed, the plastic became part of the asphalt mixture rather than remaining as loose waste. South Sioux City worked with the University of Nebraska–Lincoln, Dow Chemical Company, Jebro Waste Management, Barkley Asphalt, First Star Recycling and Goodwill of the Great Plains. A grant from the Nebraska Environmental Trust also helped fund the demonstration.South Sioux City City Administrator Lance Hedquist became involved with the project after looking at road-building experiments. Rather than treating those projects simply as something to observe, city officials began considering whether a similar approach could be tested locally. The result was a working section of Foundry Road where the material could be evaluated under ordinary conditions.According to Nebraska Public Media, Hedquist said, "We were watching some innovations that were taking place worldwide and what was happening in other countries was very beneficial.""We're making a good use out of products that are just tossed away and blowing in the environment. So we're using plastic bags in a positive way."The Foundry Road project also reflects a broader problem with materials that are difficult to keep within conventional recycling systems. A plastic bag may be used for only a short time, but the material itself does not disappear when the shopping is finished.South Sioux City's approach shifts the question from how to dispose of the bags to whether some of them can become an input for infrastructure instead. In this case, the proposed destination was asphalt.The project does not mean millions of plastic bags can simply be added to every road. The material has to be collected, processed and incorporated into a suitable asphalt mix, and the resulting pavement still needs to prove itself over time.
Article Summary: A road in South Sioux City, Nebraska, was paved with shredded plastic bags. Roughly two million bags were processed for the project, turning lightweight waste into part of a working road. The project covered roughly 4,000 feet of road, making it a relatively small-scale test rather than a citywide change.

Article Title: ‘Call it Trump Strait’: US president’s Hormuz pitch as he rallies GOP voters
Article Text:
The remarks came as Trump used his keynote address to make a broader pitch for Republican candidates and his administration’s record

US President Donald Trump turned his Republican Party’s midterm convention in Dallas into a showcase for his trademark political rhetoric on Wednesday, suggesting the Strait of Hormuz should be renamed the “Trump Strait” as he sought to rally voters behind the GOP ahead of the November elections.“I think we should call the Hormuz Strait the Trump Strait. I should get something out of it. The Trump Strait,” Trump told the crowd, referring to the strategically vital waterway amid heightened tensions with Iran.Trump also renewed his pitch for renaming Lake Ontario claiming that the water body should be called “Lake America” and suggesting New Mexico could become “New America”. “Canada very much wants to make a deal. They're dying to make a deal. But it's going to be called Lake America,” he said.The remarks came as Trump used his keynote address to make a broader pitch for Republican candidates and his administration’s record. He urged supporters to treat the upcoming midterms as though he himself were on the ballot, despite not being eligible to seek another presidential term.“If we hand America’s future to the radical-left Democrats, our nation will spend the next decade just getting back on its feet,” Trump said.“Vote Republican and we will leave the world in our dust for generations to come.”Trump said there were around 35 key Senate and House races and pledged to campaign across the states involved, promising, “We’re gonna have rallies just like this.”He also highlighted his administration’s tax policies, including “No Tax on Tips, No Tax on Overtime, and No Tax on Social Security”, while claiming that the US had attracted more than $20 trillion in foreign investment.“This has been the most successful two years financially and every other way in the history of the presidency,” Trump said.The president also defended Senate Majority Leader John Thune after the Texas crowd booed him, saying, “No, no. John is working hard. He’s got great opposition.”Trump separately praised Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is facing a competitive Senate race, while acknowledging criticism of his appearance and speaking style. “He may not talk exactly perfectly, and he may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen,” Trump said, before adding that Paxton “deserves to be your next senator.”
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump turned his Republican Party’s midterm convention in Dallas into a showcase for his trademark political rhetoric. He urged supporters to treat the upcoming midterms as though he himself were on the ballot, despite not being eligible to seek another presidential term.

Article Title: Osama bin Laden had Taliban rival assassinated 2 days before 9/11 attack
Article Text:
Osama bin Laden (File photo)

Ahmad Shah Massoud, the prominent Afghan resistance leader and one of the Taliban's strongest rivals, was assassinated on September 9, 2001, just two days before the 9/11 attacks, in a killing believed to have been ordered by al-Qaeda chief Osama bin Laden as a favour to his Taliban hosts, according to a Newsweek report.Massoud, who led Afghanistan's Northern Alliance, was killed while being interviewed at his camp in the Panjshir Valley by two men posing as Belgian television journalists. The two al-Qaeda operatives had concealed explosives inside a video camera despite undergoing security checks before meeting the resistance leader, Newsweek reported.The Northern Alliance did not officially confirm Massoud's death until September 15.Massoud had built a powerful insurgent network in northern Afghanistan and remained a major obstacle to Taliban control of the country. His influence and popularity also made him a key figure among forces opposed to the Taliban.According to Newsweek, bin Laden was believed to have ordered Massoud's assassination partly as a favour to his Taliban hosts and partly because he expected the United States to launch retaliatory strikes following the planned September 11 attacks Eliminating Massoud was also strategically important because bin Laden understood the Afghan leader's value as a military commander and political figure who could have played a significant role in any campaign against the Taliban and al-Qaeda.The assassination alarmed the CIA, which had maintained contacts with Massoud and other Afghan opposition figures.Gary Berntsen, the CIA officer who later led the agency's first team into Afghanistan after the 9/11 attacks, recalled that the news "made me feel sick to my stomach ... I figured this was the end of the Northern Alliance."CIA director George Tenet was less pessimistic, noting that the agency had maintained relationships with other Afghan warlords.Tenet later wrote, "Masood's [sic] brutal murder by al-Qaeda on the eve of the 9/11 attacks might have undone our plan before it got under way if we hadn't maintained contact with other warlords in the north."Tenet's meeting with Pakistan's ISI chiefOn the day Massoud was assassinated, Tenet was having lunch with Pakistani Gen. Mahmood Ahmed, then head of the Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), Pakistan's main intelligence agency.According to Tenet's account, he pressed Mahmood on al-Qaeda and Taliban leader Mullah Omar. Mahmood assured him that Omar wanted what was best for the Afghan people and suggested that the CIA try bribing key Taliban officials to secure bin Laden's surrender."As gracious as he could be over the lunch table, the guy was immovable when it came to the Taliban and al-Qaeda," Tenet later wrote.Mahmood would be in Washington on September 11, when he met senior US lawmakers including Senate Intelligence Committee chairman Bob Graham, House Intelligence Committee chairman Porter Goss and Senator Jon Kyl.In the aftermath of the attacks, Mahmood held further meetings with US officials as Washington pressed Pakistan to cooperate in its campaign against terrorism. US military forces were also clandestinely deployed to Pakistani territory as the Bush administration prepared its response to the attacks.Massoud's assassination therefore came at a critical moment. Two days before the attacks that transformed US foreign policy and triggered the war in Afghanistan, one of the Taliban's most formidable opponents had already been eliminated.
Article Summary: Ahmad Shah Massoud was assassinated on September 9, 2001, two days before the 9/11 attacks. Massoud led Afghanistan's Northern Alliance and was a major obstacle to Taliban control. Al-Qaeda chief Osama bin Laden believed to have ordered Massoud's assassination.

Article Title: BLA claims 52 Pakistani personnel killed in 28 operations across Balochistan
Article Text:
BLA claims major offensive across Balochistan, 52 Pakistani personnel killed in 28 operations

The Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) has claimed that it carried out 28 operations across Balochistan between September 1 and 7, killing 52 Pakistani military personnel and injuring several others.The claims come against the backdrop of separate military operations in the province, with the Pakistani Army saying security forces killed 11 militants in Kharan and Washuk districts on September 6 and 7.According to the Balochistan Post, in a weekly statement, BLA spokesperson Jeeyand Baloch said the group conducted operations in Pasni, Kharan, Kalat, Turbat, Mastung, Surab, Tump, Pishin, Jhal Magsi, Noshki, Chagai and Quetta. The group also said 12 of its rebels were killed during clashes with Pakistani forces.The BLA’s account, as reported by TBP, began with an operation on September 1 at Zero Point in Pasni, Gwadar. The group claimed that it attacked a joint police and Levies post and checkpoints operated by Customs and the Coastal Police, seized weapons and military equipment, and later destroyed the positions.It said an ambush on a convoy at Albat in Kharan and an attack at Garari in Kalat targeted personnel transporting armoured vehicles, with three vehicles severely damaged and personnel killed or injured.On September 2, the group claimed an IED attack followed by an ambush at Guro in Mastung’s Khadkocha area, alleging four personnel were killed and more than seven injured. A day later, it claimed an STOS attack at Hajika in Surab, killing seven personnel and destroying one vehicle.The BLA claimed its Fateh Squad killed 18 Pakistani military personnel and injured five in Pishin’s Ziarat Cross. It also claimed attacks in Tump, Mastung, Kalat and Jhal Magsi, and took responsibility for the killings of Abdul Rehman Langove and Rehmat Saeed in Quetta, alleging both worked for Pakistani forces.Separately, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the Pakistani Army’s media wing, said eight militants were killed in Kharan on September 6 after security forces intercepted a group allegedly attempting to block a road. Another three were killed in Washuk the following day, it said.The BLA’s casualty and operational claims have not been independently verified.Meanwhile, TBP reported two fresh alleged enforced disappearances in Balochistan, while five previously missing people had returned home. It said Ali Baloch was allegedly detained by Pakistani forces in Mastung on August 23 and remains unaccounted for.
Article Summary: Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) claims it carried out 28 operations across Balochistan between September 1 and 7. BLA claims 52 Pakistani military personnel killed in 28 operations. Pakistani Army says security forces killed 11 militants in Kharan and Washuk districts.

Article Title: Pakistan orders medical institutions to expel Afghan students, halt fresh admissions amid Kabul tensions
Article Text:
Afghan students face expulsion from Pakistan medical colleges amid rising tensions

Poll Vote & Share your view Should Afghan students already enrolled be allowed to continue their studies in Pakistan? Yes, they should be allowed No, they should return to Afghanistan 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI: Pakistan has ordered medical and dental institutions across the country to stop admitting Afghan students and remove those already enrolled, amid worsening relations between Islamabad and Kabul, a senior government official said on Wednesday.The decision could affect hundreds of Afghan students pursuing undergraduate medical and dental courses in Pakistan, including students close to completing their degrees.Under a directive issued to medical and dental institutions, the Pakistan Medical and Dental Council has barred colleges from admitting or placing Afghan students during the current academic session, a senior health ministry official said.Afghan students already enrolled in medical and dental programmes have also been instructed to return to Afghanistan, the official said.The measure applies specifically to Afghan nationals and does not affect students from other countries, the official added. He said the decision was taken against the backdrop of deteriorating relations between the two neighbouring countries.However, Pakistan's Foreign Office said Afghan students who hold valid travel and residency documents can continue to apply for visa extensions under existing rules.Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan told Dawn that under Pakistan's Illegal Foreigners Repatriation Plan, foreign nationals without valid passports and visas are staying in the country illegally and can be deported.“However, Pakistani authorities are continuing to process visa extension applications from Afghan students in accordance with our existing policy, rules and regulations,” he said.King Edward Medical University (KEMU) in Lahore has become the first public-sector institution to implement the directive, according to a university official.“Twenty-two Afghan students are currently studying at KEMU, and they have been given 24 hours to complete the necessary legal and administrative formalities,” the official told PTI.The order comes as tensions between Islamabad and Kabul remain high, particularly over Pakistan's allegations that the banned Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan operates from sanctuaries in Afghanistan. The Taliban administration has denied the allegation.Relations deteriorated further following a series of explosions in Kabul on October 9 last year and subsequent cross-border exchanges that resulted in casualties and damage on both sides.The latest order comes against the backdrop of Pakistan's broader campaign to deport Afghan nationals without valid documentation.Millions of Afghans have sought refuge in Pakistan over several decades after fleeing successive conflicts. Hundreds of thousands more entered the country after the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan in 2021.Pakistan launched a large-scale deportation drive against undocumented foreigners in 2023 and renewed the campaign in April last year after cancelling hundreds of thousands of residence permits held by Afghan nationals.In June, Pakistan's interior ministry directed authorities to arrest Afghan nationals found living in the country without valid visas from July 10.More than one million Afghan nationals were deported from Pakistan last year alone.
Article Summary: Pakistan has ordered medical and dental institutions across the country to stop admitting Afghan students and remove those already enrolled. The decision comes amid worsening relations between Islamabad and Kabul. Pakistan's Foreign Office said Afghan students who hold valid travel and residency documents can continue to apply for visa extensions.

Article Title: 'Attack on one is attack on all': Pakistan warns Houthis, invokes Mecca defence pact
Article Text:
Pakistan warns Houthis that its defence alliance with Saudi Arabia and Turkey

Poll Vote & Share your view What is your opinion on the recent Houthi missile attacks on Saudi Arabia? Justified retaliation Unprovoked aggression Escalation of conflict 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Pakistan warned Tuesday that its newly formed defence alliance with Saudi Arabia and Turkiye could be activated if the conflict in Yemen spills into Saudi territory, saying there should be “no ambiguity” that an attack on any one of the three members would be treated as an attack on all.Pakistan’s defence minister Khawaja Asif said the agreement signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye in Makkah last month was defensive in nature and required the three countries to respond if any member came under unprovoked aggression.“There should be no ambiguity; there is no need for any clarity that this is a joint defence agreement,” Asif said in an interview with Geo TV. He added that Pakistan was “bound by the terms and conditions of this pact” and would honour its commitments to Saudi Arabia if required.His comments came hours after Iran-aligned Houthi forces launched a wave of missile and drone attacks on southern Saudi Arabia, targeting cities as well as economic and energy infrastructure. At least 73 civilians were injured, according to the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen.Asif stressed that the alliance did not give its members a mandate to launch offensive operations against another country on their own initiative.“This is not an aggressive agreement under which the three countries would, on their own initiative, attack another country. But if there is any aggression against one member state, all three member states will respond,” he said.The minister said he was not aware of any contact between Islamabad and Riyadh following the latest Houthi attacks. He also expressed hope that tensions would ease, while warning the Houthis against extending the Yemen conflict into Saudi Arabia.“If they try to export them, the clauses of this agreement to counter aggression will become operative,” Asif said.Pakistan prime minister Shehbaz Sharif separately condemned the Houthi attacks, describing them as “cowardly” and saying they threatened civilian lives as well as regional peace and security. He said Pakistan stood in “unwavering” solidarity with Saudi Arabia and reaffirmed support for the kingdom's sovereignty, security and territorial integrity.The Saudi-led coalition said the attacks had temporarily disrupted operations at some targeted sites, while specialised teams worked to contain fires and secure the facilities. Riyadh also warned against continued attacks on civilians and commercial shipping.The Houthis said the attacks were retaliation for recent Saudi airstrikes on areas of northwestern Yemen under their control. The group had also accused Saudi Arabia of bombing a prison in Al Hazm on Monday, killing at least 11 people.Asif described the Houthis as “non-state actors” and said sympathy for Iran's position in its ongoing conflict with the United States existed across parts of the Muslim world, including Yemen. But he cautioned against allowing those sentiments to widen the conflict.He also said the Mecca alliance could act as a deterrent without necessarily requiring a military response to every attack.“We don't need to respond to a brick with a stone,” Asif said, arguing that the combined military capabilities of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye should themselves serve as a deterrent.
Article Summary: Pakistan warns Houthis that its defence alliance with Saudi Arabia and Turkey could be activated if the conflict in Yemen spills into Saudi territory. Pakistan’s defence minister Khawaja Asif said the agreement was defensive in nature and required the three countries to respond if any member came under unprovoked aggression.

Article Title: 'Break pattern of impunity': UN experts flag persecution of Pakistan's Ahmadiyya community
Article Text:
Poll Vote & Share your view How should the Pakistani government address human rights violations against minorities? Strengthen laws and policies Increase community awareness programs Collaborate with international organizations All of the above 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

United Nations experts have expressed concerns over reports of human rights violations against members of the Ahmadiyya Muslim community in Pakistan and urged authorities to ensure their protection.According to an official release, the experts said, "We are deeply concerned by persistent reports that members of the Ahmadiyya community continue to face harassment, criminal prosecution, violence, and exclusion because of their religious identity.""Every individual has the right to freedom of thought, conscience, religion or belief. No one should be subjected to discrimination, intimidation, or violence, nor should they be prevented from peacefully manifesting their faith or face discrimination with respect to any of their human rights," they added.Experts also highlighted ongoing attacks on Ahmadi places of worship; desecration of graves; interference with peaceful religious observance, including in the context of Eid-ul-Fitr and Eid-ul-Adha; arrests and prosecutions related to religious practices or identity; and hate speech."The State has a responsibility to exercise due diligence to prevent human rights violations, investigate allegations promptly and impartially, prosecute those responsible in accordance with international standards, and provide effective remedies to victims," the experts said.“Pakistan must break the pattern of impunity that has allowed perpetrators of attacks and incitement to hatred and violence to act without restraint,” they said. “These attacks take place with tacit official complicity, whilst the cycle of fear prevents people and institutions from upholding the rights and dignity of these minority groups.”They called on the Pakistan government to ensure that all individuals, regardless of their religion or belief, enjoy equal protection under the law without discrimination. The experts also urged the government to review legislation and administrative measures that may be inconsistent with its obligations under international human rights law, including the rights to freedom of religion or belief, freedom of expression, freedom of association and assembly, cultural rights, and equality before the law."Combating religious intolerance requires more than responding to individual incidents," the release cited them as saying. "It requires sustained efforts to foster respect for diversity, counter incitement to hatred and violence, and create an environment in which all religious or belief communities can live in safety and dignity."
Article Summary: U.N. experts have expressed concerns over reports of human rights violations against members of the Ahmadiyya Muslim community in Pakistan. The experts urged authorities to ensure their protection. They highlighted ongoing attacks on Ahmadi places of worship and desecration of graves.

Article Title: Balochistan’s Zehri under curfew: Civilian killings, detentions and disappearances; what we know
Article Text:
Pakistan's enforced disappearance crisis deepens as four reported missing in Balochistan. Photo credit: ANI

Earlier allegations and UN concerns

A prolonged curfew and reported military operation in Zehri tehsil of Pakistan’s Balochistan province have triggered fresh allegations of detentions, enforced disappearances and civilian casualties.According to a report by The Balochistan Post, Pakistani security forces detained around 25 residents from the Sunni area during the operation and allegedly subjected them to enforced disappearance. Quoting sources,news agency ANI reported that a woman was also killed in a quadcopter attack while she was collecting water, while another woman and a man were wounded.Mobile phone services have reportedly been suspended across Zehri, while residents face restrictions on movement. The Balochistan Post said the area has remained under curfew for months, with residents allowed to leave only during designated hours to purchase essential goods. Travel outside the area reportedly requires authorisation from security forces.The Post also reported that Pakistani forces had allegedly killed more than 20 civilians during an operation in the Sohanda area while the curfew was in force.The latest allegations follow a series of reported enforced disappearances elsewhere in Balochistan.On September 2, the local media reported that four people had allegedly gone missing after being detained in Quetta and Dera Bugti, while four previously reported missing persons were recovered from Karachi, Quetta and Hyderabad.The issue has also drawn concern from UN human rights experts. On Saturday, the Office of the UN high commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) raised concerns over the alleged enforced disappearance, torture and extrajudicial killing of Imran Ali.The UN experts said Ali was abducted from his apartment on August 27, 2025, by around 20 personnel from Pakistan’s Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD). They said people previously detained with him later confirmed that he had been held and allegedly tortured.A police officer reportedly told Pakistan’s Commission of Inquiry on Enforced Disappearances in August 2026 that Ali had been killed during an alleged encounter in May. The UN experts called for an independent investigation, forensic examination and identification of six other bodies reportedly brought to a hospital alongside his remains.Meanwhile, Pakistan’s military said on Friday that its forces had killed 48 militants in raids across Mastung, Sibi, Quetta and Kalat over 72 hours, describing those killed as “Khawarij” and “terrorists” without providing evidence, AP reported.
Article Summary: A prolonged curfew and reported military operation in Zehri tehsil of Pakistan’s Balochistan province have triggered fresh allegations of detentions, enforced disappearances and civilian casualties. Pakistani security forces detained around 25 residents from the Sunni area during the operation and allegedly subjected them to enforced disappearance. A woman was also killed in a quadcopter attack while she was collecting water.

Article Title: ‘Growing differences between military, Asif Zardari’: Self-exiled Pakistani politician Altaf Hussain makes big claim
Article Text:
Self-exiled British-Pakistani politician Altaf Hussain (File photo)

Self-exiled British-Pakistani politician Altaf Hussain has alleged a "silent struggle" is underway between Pakistan's powerful military establishment and President Asif Ali Zardari , warning that a debate over creating new provinces could push the country into a major political and security crisis.The founder of the Muttahida Qaumi Movement (MQM) claimed that discussions were underway on a possible 28th Constitutional Amendment, which could include provisions for the creation of new provinces.“Discussions on the creation of new provinces have been raised by interior minister Mohsin Naqvi and DG-ISPR. The proposed constitutional changes reflect growing differences between President Asif Ali Zardari and the military leadership. A political deadlock could lead to serious constitutional consequences, including the imposition of martial law or the formation of an interim government,” Hussain said in a TikTok message on September 2.Referring to the earlier 26th and 27th Amendments, he alleged that political parties had previously reached agreements to facilitate their passage.Hussain also questioned the prolonged foreign stay of Zardari, the husband of slain former Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto and father of ex-foreign minister Bilawal Bhutto Zardari."The President had travelled to Austria in connection for his son Bilawal Zardari’s wedding and is currently in London. There was also an hour-long meeting between Zardari and Naqvi in London, claiming that an important message was conveyed to the President," he added.Hussain further cautioned that tensions between the Pakistan military and Sindhi nationalist groups could escalate into widespread unrest. Referring to the situation in Balochistan, Hussain said violence between security forces and Baloch fighters was continuing and called for greater political consideration for the Baloch people.He warned that if Pakistan descended into a broader civil conflict, foreign powers, including the US and UK, would not come to its rescue, and urged Pakistanis to heed his warnings.
Article Summary: Self-exiled British-Pakistani politician Altaf Hussain has alleged a "silent struggle" is underway between Pakistan's powerful military establishment and President Asif Ali Zardari. The founder of the Muttahida Qaumi Movement (MQM) claimed that discussions were underway on a possible 28th Constitutional Amendment.

Article Title: 25 Pakistani military personnel killed in Balochistan attacks, BLA claims
Article Text:
Balochistan: BLA claims 25 Pakistani military personnel killed in two attacks (Picture from X)

The Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) on Thursday claimed responsibility for two attacks in Pakistan’s Balochistan province, saying 25 Pakistani military personnel were killed and three military vehicles destroyed.According to The Balochistan Post, the BLA spokesperson said fighters targeted a military convoy at Ziarat Cross, attacking vehicles and destroying two of them, including a military truck.The militant group initially claimed that 18 personnel were killed in the attack, with the death toll later rising to 25.The BLA also released a one-minute-and-11-second video trailer through Hakkal, its official media channel, which it said showed footage from the Ziarat Cross attack.The footage purportedly shows armed fighters near burning Pakistani military vehicles, with bodies visible at the site and weapons being seized. The BLA said it would release the complete video later.In a separate operation in the Hajika area of Surab, the group’s Special Tactical Operations Squad (STOS) remotely detonated an explosives-laden vehicle, destroying a military vehicle and killing seven personnel, according to the BLA statement.
Article Summary: Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) claims responsibility for two attacks in Pakistan's Balochistan province. BLA says 25 Pakistani military personnel were killed and three military vehicles destroyed. The militant group also released a one-minute-and-11-second video trailer through Hakkal.

Article Title: ‘6ft by 8ft cell, brown drinking water’: What Imran Khan’s jail cell is like
Article Text:
The report said visitors have been barred and Khan has been confined to his cell for as much as 23 hours a day.

Former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan is being held in what has been described as harsh conditions at Rawalpindi’s Adiala Jail, with reports alleging prolonged isolation, limited access to reading material and restrictions on contact with his family.According to a report by The Times UK, Khan is being kept in a 6ft by 8ft cell typically used for prisoners on death row. The report said the 73-year-old has no reading material apart from the Quran and is being provided “soiled brown water” to drink.His sons, Sulaiman and Kasim Khan, have reportedly been unable to meet their father in person since 2022 and have at times been prevented from speaking to him by telephone for months. They have described his living conditions as inhumane “torture tactics”.The report said visitors have been barred and Khan has been confined to his cell for as much as 23 hours a day.The reported restrictions have also become the subject of repeated legal challenges by Khan’s family.His sister Uzma Khan filed a fresh contempt petition in the Supreme Court on Wednesday, alleging that authorities have failed to comply with an August 18 order concerning Khan’s access to his family.According to The Express Tribune, the petition names Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Adiala Jail Superintendent Sajid Baig, Punjab Inspector General of Prisons Mian Salik Jalal and other senior officials as respondents.The August 18 order had directed authorities to facilitate virtual communication between Khan and his sons and allow his sisters to meet him weekly. However, Uzma said she was denied a scheduled visit on Tuesday, while telephone communication between Khan and his sons has remained restricted since March.The petition also alleges that authorities failed to establish the infrastructure required for bi-weekly telephone calls with Sulaiman and Kasim.The latest dispute follows an earlier contempt petition over the alleged non-compliance with the Supreme Court’s direction to transfer Khan to Shifa International Hospital for medical evaluation. He was instead taken to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) on August 21 before being returned to Adiala Jail after doctors declared him “medically fit”. Authorities have cited security concerns for the decision.
Article Summary: Imran Khan is being held in what has been described as harsh conditions at Rawalpindi’s Adiala Jail. Reports allege prolonged isolation, limited access to reading material and restrictions on contact with his family. His sons, Sulaiman and Kasim Khan, have reportedly been unable to meet their father in person since 2022.

Article Title: Pakistan: Imran Khan's sister files fresh contempt plea over denied jail visits
Article Text: Former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan's sister Uzma Khan on Wednesday filed a fresh contempt of court petition in the Supreme Court, alleging non-enforcement of previous judicial directives issued by the country's apex court.In her petition, Uzma named several high-ranking officials, including Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif and Adiala (Rawalpindi Central Jail) Superintendent Sajid Baig, as respondents.According to the Express Tribune, the petition was filed after the Supreme Court's August 18 instructions, which mandated virtual communication between Imran Khan and his sons, alongside weekly access for his sisters, failed to materialise.The plea said that Uzma Khan was denied a scheduled visit on Tuesday and noted that audio communication with his sons has remained restricted since March.The petition alleged that authorities neglected to establish the necessary infrastructure enabling bi-weekly telephone calls with his sons, Kasim Khan and Sulaiman Khan, as previously ordered by the bench.Earlier, Uzma had filed another contempt application addressing government non-compliance regarding a separate instruction within the August 18 order, which directed that Imran Khan be moved to Shifa International Hospital for medical care.Under the original August 18 decision, the Supreme Court instructed that the former premier be transferred to Shifa International Hospital for clinical evaluation by a multidisciplinary medical panel while simultaneously granting visitation rights.Following the orders, authorities transferred Imran Khan to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) on August 21. He was, however, sent back to Adiala Jail shortly after medical personnel declared him to be "medically fit".Reacting to the developments, the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) lambasted prison administrators for barring relatives from seeing the party founder, characterising the restrictions as a flagrant breach of mandates issued by both the Supreme Court and the Islamabad High Court, as reported by another Pakistan-based daily, Dawn.
Article Summary: Imran Khan's sister Uzma Khan has filed a contempt of court petition in the Supreme Court. She alleges non-enforcement of previous judicial directives issued by the country's apex court. Uzma named several high-ranking officials, including Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif and Adiala (Rawalpindi Central Jail) Superintendent Sajid Baig as respondents.

Article Title: Pak pleads for dialogue after India stands firm on suspending Indus Water Treaty
Article Text:
Indus Waters treaty representational image

India rejects tribunal ruling

Water, terrorism and the SCO

NEW DELHI: Just days after India rejected an international tribunal's ruling on the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) and dismissed its jurisdiction, Pakistan on Wednesday urged New Delhi to engage "constructively" within the framework of the 1960 water-sharing agreement.According to news agency PTI, Pakistan foreign office spokesperson Tahir Andrabi said the Permanent Court of Arbitration had reaffirmed that the treaty remained fully enforced and binding. Pakistan, he said, would take “all possible measures” to ensure the decision was implemented.Andrabi said Pakistan remained committed to implementing the treaty in letter and spirit in accordance with its language and provisions.Pakistan will continue to urge India to reciprocate with the same approach whereby the treaty is upheld in letter and spirit and in its full legal documented provisions, he said, according to PTI.Pakistan had approached the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague in March 2026, seeking a determination on the status of the treaty after India placed it in abeyance.India, however, has consistently rejected the jurisdiction of the arbitration process.On Monday, the ministry of external affairs (MEA) said, “India categorically rejects its so-called award, just as it has firmly rejected all prior pronouncements by this illegally constituted body.”“India's decision to hold the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance remains in force,” the ministry said.MEA said the Court of Arbitration had issued what it termed an award on May 15, 2026, concerning maximum pondage supplemental to an earlier award on issues of general interpretation of the IWT."This so-called Court was constituted by the World Bank in patent breach of the terms of the Treaty and India categorically rejects its so-called award, just as it has firmly rejected all prior pronouncements by this illegally constituted body", the ministry stated.India has maintained that the establishment of the arbitral body itself violates the IWT and that it has no jurisdiction over India’s sovereign decision to place the treaty in abeyance.The dispute also featured indirectly at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit, in Bishkek, where Prime Minister Narendra Modi called for action against countries that use terrorism as an instrument of state policy.“We cannot remain confined to an action-reaction approach,” Modi said, calling for the dismantling of terrorist ecosystems, including funding networks, recruitment pipelines and territorial sanctuaries.Pakistan prime minister Shehbaz Sharif, speaking at the summit, described water as the region’s “lifeblood” and said it “must never be weaponised”.“The treaties governing our shared waters are solemn, binding international commitments. They are not matters of political convenience to be cast aside at your will. They must be honoured unconditionally, in both letter and spirit,” Sharif said, according to Dawn.India placed the IWT in abeyance following the April 22, 2025 Pahalgam terror attack, in which 26 people were killed. The Cabinet Committee on Security took the decision on April 23, 2025, with New Delhi saying the conditions underlying the treaty had fundamentally changed.India has said the treaty will remain in abeyance until Pakistan “credibly and irrevocably abjures its support for cross-border terrorism”.
Article Summary: Pakistan urges New Delhi to engage "constructively" within the framework of the 1960 water-sharing agreement. Pakistan had approached the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague in March 2026, seeking a determination on the status of the treaty. India, however, has consistently rejected the jurisdiction of the arbitration process.

Article Title: Leadership gaps cloud Pakistan's human rights oversight system
Article Text:
Pakistan human rights faces pending vacancy

NCHR’s legal status under question

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is most important for an effective human rights body? Strong leadership Independence Transparency Accountability 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Pakistan’s human rights oversight framework is facing growing uncertainty as key commissions continue to function without permanent leadership or full membership, raising concerns over their independence and effectiveness.The previous National Commission for Human Rights (NCHR) completed its four-year term in November 2025, but a new commission has yet to be fully constituted, news agency ANI cited in its report. The National Commission on the Status of Women (NCSW) is also functioning under an acting chairperson.Former NCHR chairperson Khawar Mumtaz criticised and warned that prolonged reliance on temporary arrangements could weaken the autonomy and performance of independent rights bodies.Human rights activist Peter Jacob said Parliament passed legislation establishing the National Commission for Minorities Rights in December 2025, but appointments to the body remain incomplete.The National Commission on the Rights of the Child has also faced vacancies. The Ministry of Human Rights invited applications in July 2026 for members representing Punjab, Islamabad and Balochistan, The Express Tribune reported.An amendment to the National Commission for Human Rights Act in 2026 introduced Section 4A, allowing a chairperson to continue for up to 120 days after the expiry of their term or until a successor is appointed.NCHR Chairperson Rabiya Javeri Agha maintained that the commission remains operationally effective, pointing to additional staff recruited two years ago. She said the extension of the chairperson’s tenure was made under the law and reflected practices followed by human rights institutions internationally. Questions regarding the constitution of a new commission, she said, should be directed to the government, according to The Express Tribune.
Article Summary: Pakistan’s human rights oversight framework is facing growing uncertainty. Key commissions continue to function without permanent leadership or full membership. The previous National Commission for Human Rights (NCHR) completed its four-year term in November 2025. A new commission has yet to be fully constituted, news agency ANI cited in its report.

Article Title: Imran Khan, wife Bushra Bibi get slight relief as Pak HC bars solitary confinement
Article Text:
Pak HC intervenes over Imran Khan, wife Bushra Bibi's detention, bars solitary confinement

A Pakistan high court on Tuesday directed authorities at Rawalpindi Jail to ensure that former prime minister Imran Khan and his wife Bushra Bibi are not held in solitary confinement. The ruling also set out provisions for Khan's family meetings, phone calls, reading material and medical care.The Islamabad High Court (IHC), while hearing petitions challenging the couple's alleged solitary confinement, directed the jail authorities to allow Khan's family members to meet him in line with prison rules and arrange telephone conversations with his sons.Justice Khadim Hussain Soomro also ordered the jail to provide Khan with newspapers and books every day and ensure access to medical facilities as prescribed under jail rules. Rawalpindi's Aiala jail superintendent has been asked to implement the directions and submit a compliance report within 15 days, according to the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI).The court had earlier reserved its verdict on August 6 on separate petitions filed by Khan's sister Aleema Khanum and Bushra Bibi's daughter Mubashra Khawar Maneka. The IHC also held the petitions challenging the alleged solitary confinement to be maintainable.The 73-year-old cricketer-turned-politician and his wife have been in custody since August 2023 and is serving prison terms in corruption and related cases. Khan's Tehreek-e-Insaf party and supporters have maintained that the cases are politically motivated, while the government has rejected allegations of mistreatment.Bushra Bibi was first jailed in January 2024 after being convicted in a corruption-related case. She was released on bail in October that year after nearly nine months in custody but was arrested again in January 2025 following another corruption conviction. She remains at Adiala Jail.The IHC order comes as Khan's detention and medical treatment remain the subject of separate proceedings before the Supreme Court.On Monday, the Supreme Court declined an application by Khan's sister Uzma Khan seeking an early hearing of her contempt petition against government officials over the alleged failure to comply with an earlier order concerning his transfer to a private hospital, Dawn reported.Pakistan's Supreme Court had on August 18 ordered that Khan be shifted to the privately run Shifa International Hospital after concerns were raised by his family and supporters over his health, including an eye condition diagnosed earlier this year.Instead, Khan was taken to the state-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) on the night of August 20-21 for a medical procedure and diagnostic examinations and was later returned to Adiala Jail.Uzma Khan's petition contends that this breached the Supreme Court's direction that Khan remain admitted at the Islamabad hospital until the next hearing on September 16. The government has defended the decision, citing security concerns.Two specialists from Shifa International Hospital also participated in Khan's eye examination at PIMS, according to the hospital administration, as reported by Dawn.Uzma Khan had sought an earlier hearing, arguing that further delay could affect the enforcement of the Supreme Court's order. The Supreme Court, however, rejected the request under its case-fixation policy, noting that 94 other criminal original petitions in the same category were pending, Dawn reported.The contempt petition is listed for September 16 before a three-member bench comprising Justices Shahid Waheed, Naeem Akhtar Afghan and Ishtiaq Ibrahim. The bench is also scheduled to hear other matters concerning Khan's health and family meetings.
Article Summary: Imran Khan and his wife Bushra Bibi have been in custody since August 2023. The couple is serving prison terms in corruption and related cases. The Islamabad High Court ordered the jail authorities to allow Khan's family members to meet him in line with prison rules.

Article Title: Pakistan power crisis deepens as Karachi reels from 24-hour blackouts
Article Text:
​Karachi reels under deepening power crisis as blackouts last up to 24 hours

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you agree that electricity should be treated as an essential service? Yes No Unsure 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Karachi's electricity crisis has intensified, with residents in several parts of the city reporting outages lasting up to 24 hours. Rights activists in Pakistan have warned that prolonged loadshedding is placing a growing burden on low-income families.According to Dawn, the issue was raised at a press conference at the Karachi Press Club organised by the Civil Society Collective for Clean Energy for Karachi. Speakers said extended power cuts were disrupting basic household activities, education and work, while also worsening access to water and affecting hygiene.Residents of North Karachi, Nazimabad and parts of Gulistan-i-Jauhar reported between 16 and 24 hours of loadshedding, ANI said. Protests and traffic disruptions were also reported in Lyari and other parts of the old city during the week beginning August 24.The speakers cited K-Electric's published outage schedule, saying more than 615 feeders were listed for power cuts of up to 12 hours a day. They claimed this could affect nearly a third of the city's feeders.Qazi Khizer of the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan said the prolonged outages were having a particularly severe impact on working-class communities.He said electricity shortages were also contributing to rising mental stress and argued that reliable electricity "should be treated as an essential service rather than a privilege".Karachi Union of Journalists president Tahir Hassan Khan questioned whether K-Electric's privatisation had delivered the improvements promised to consumers.He said claims of technological and operational progress had not translated into "dependable electricity supplies".
Article Summary: Residents of North Karachi, Nazimabad and parts of Gulistan-i-Jauhar reported between 16 and 24 hours of loadshedding. Protests and traffic disruptions were also reported in Lyari and other parts of the old city during the week beginning August 24.

Article Title: Pakistan court allows Hindu woman to return home after alleged forced conversion, marriage
Article Text:
Woman returns from Pakistan

'Want to return home'

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you believe that the court made the right decision in allowing Reeta to return to her parents? Yes, it was the right decision. No, she should have been placed in shelter. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

A court in Pakistan on Tuesday allowed a 21-year-old Hindu woman to return to her parents after she told the magistrate that she wished to go home of her own free will, days after her family alleged that she had been abducted and pressured to convert to Islam and marry a Muslim man, news agency PTI reported.Shirimati Reeta, a resident of Rana Rajput Colony in Khipro tehsil of Sindh’s Sanghar district, went missing from her hometown last week, according to a complaint filed by her brother Ravi Shankar. He alleged that CCTV footage showed unidentified people taking Reeta from the family home along with valuables and mobile phones on August 24.According to the complaint, Reeta was taken to Gujranwala in Punjab, some 80 kms from Lahore, where she was allegedly pressured to convert to Islam and marry Nazeer Hussain, who was already married.Punjab Police later recovered Reeta and produced her before a judicial magistrate on Monday. The investigating officer sought to place her in Darul Aman, a state-run shelter, claiming that she was unwilling to return to her parents.Her lawyers, Asad Jamal and Kheta Ram, opposed the request and told the court that Reeta wanted to return home with her brother, who was present in court, a court official said.The magistrate then asked Reeta to record her statement under oath. “In her statement, Reeta said that she wanted to return to her parents’ home of her own free will,” the official said.The court subsequently allowed Reeta to leave with her brother and made him responsible for her safe custody and transportation back to the family home in Sanghar.
Article Summary: Shirimati Reeta, a 21-year-old Hindu woman, went missing from her hometown last week. Her family alleged that she had been abducted and pressured to convert to Islam and marry a Muslim man. Police later recovered Reeta and produced her before a judicial magistrate on Monday. The investigating officer sought to place her in Darul Aman, a state-run shelter.

Article Title: Watch: 'Driverless' car crashes into police van after internet outage in Islamabad
Article Text:
In a social media post on Monday, Aalijah sought to clarify that his video was not intended to ridicule Zafar or undermine his work and warned that the technology was not yet ready to be considered completely reliable.

A remotely operated driverless car crashed into a police van in Islamabad after losing its internet connection during a demonstration, with footage of the incident going viral and sparking a wave of memes online.According to local media, the incident took place at D-Chowk, a high-security area in the Pakistani capital, where journalist Muhammad Aalijah was recording a video of a technology-based automated-driving system developed by Abbottabad-based technology enthusiast Ehsan Zafar. The car was being controlled remotely over the internet when a sudden connectivity failure caused its steering to malfunction.Footage shared by Aalijah shows him sitting in the front passenger seat as he explains the vehicle's features while it moves along the road. The remotely controlled steering wheel then appears to lose control, sending the car towards a police van parked nearby.Aalijah can be seen attempting to stop the vehicle by pulling the handbrake, but the car continues moving and bumps into the police vehicle.Aalijah later told Dawn that he had been asked by Zafar to report on his technology-based automated-driving innovation. He attributed the crash to a "technical fault" triggered by an internet disruption.“Everything was fine until a technical fault occurred due to an internet disruption, causing the car to go out of control and crash into a police vehicle,” he said.According to Aalijah, the vehicle was operated remotely through internet and satellite connections. The loss of the internet connection during the demonstration caused the car to become uncontrollable.In a social media post on Monday, Aalijah sought to clarify that his video was not intended to ridicule Zafar or undermine his work.“The sole purpose was to raise awareness and urge people to remain cautious until any new experiment or technology has been thoroughly tested, proven safe and established as a complete success,” he said.“This was a message of caution, not an attempt to discredit anyone.”Aalijah also warned that the technology was not yet ready to be considered completely reliable.“The vehicle was being operated through satellite and internet connections, but during external control, it went out of control as soon as the internet connection was disconnected and collided with a police vehicle,” he wrote.He said the relatively low traffic at D-Chowk limited the potential consequences of the malfunction, but warned that a similar failure on a busy road could have been far more serious.“If the same situation had occurred on a busy road, the consequences could have been extremely dangerous, even fatal,” he said.“This video is not criticism; it is a responsible effort to raise awareness and issue a warning by all means, experiment, but ensure safety first,” he added.
Article Summary: A remotely operated driverless car crashed into a police van in Islamabad after losing its internet connection during a demonstration. The incident took place at D-Chowk, a high-security area in the Pakistani capital. The car was being controlled remotely over the internet when a sudden connectivity failure caused its steering to malfunction. Footage of the incident went viral and sparked a wave of memes online.

Article Title: Nepal floods: Survivor captures horrifying moment flash floods engulf homes, roads and buildings
Article Text:
New video of catastrophic Nepal floods surface

NEW DELHI: A new video from Nepal appears to capture the terrifying moments as flash floodwaters surge through a settlement, sweeping away houses, buildings and parts of a road while people scramble for higher ground. Students can be seen inside what appears to be a school building as the water level of a nearby river rises rapidly.The footage was uploaded on the Facebook page of Nepal7 media outlet and appears to have been recorded from inside a school, where several students are initially seen. Within minutes, floodwaters surge through a stream close to the building, carrying boulders, debris and water, while nearby buildings and a road on which vehicles had been travelling appear to be swept away and submerged. As the torrent intensifies, the person recording the footage and the students move up the stairs inside the building to reach higher ground.The video comes as Nepal continues to deal with the aftermath of devastating flash floods that authorities said had killed 1,356 people by Monday.According to Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA), rescue teams were still searching for 4,996 people, including at least 589 foreign nationals.Around 13,400 people had been rescued.The floods were triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, according to authorities. The resulting surge travelled downstream through the Bhotekoshi River, sweeping away homes, vehicles, roads and bridges and damaging hydropower projects.The disaster also affected neighbouring Tibet and China. Chinese media reports said at least 43 people were killed on the Chinese side, while more than 500 remained missing in Tibet.NDRRMA said 363 bodies had been recovered in Chitwan, 223 in Nawalparasi East, 221 in Nawalparasi West, 197 in Nuwakot, 169 in Rasuwa, 75 in Gorkha, 70 in Dhading and 38 in Tanahu.Identifying the dead has remained a major challenge. Only 98 bodies had been identified and handed over to families by Monday, according to NDRRMA. Nepal Police has been collecting DNA samples from relatives of missing people to help identify unclaimed remains.More than 1,000 unidentified bodies have been buried after DNA samples were collected for future identification, officials said.Nepal observed a national day of mourning on Monday, marking the continuing toll of the disaster.
Article Summary: Students can be seen inside what appears to be a school building as the water level of a nearby river rises rapidly. Rescue teams are still searching for 4,996 people, including at least 589 foreign nationals. The floods were triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26.
